Title: Potential Roles of Large Language Models in the Production of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
Snippet: A systematic review is the result of a systematic and rigorous evaluation of evidence, and a metaanalysis may or may not be a part of it [1].Due to its strict methodology and comprehensive summary of evidence, high-quality systematic reviews are considered the highest level of evidence in the hierarchy of evidence [2].They are positioned at the top of the evidence pyramid [2].

Additionally, high-quality systematic reviews and meta-analyses are often used to support the development of clinical practice guidelines, aid clinical decision-making, and inform healthcare policy formulation [3].Currently, the methods of systematic reviews and meta-analyses are also applied in various disciplines beyond medicine, such as law [4], management [5], economics [6], and have yielded positive results, contributing to the continuous advancement of these fields [7].

The process of conducting systematic reviews demands a substantial investment in terms of time, resources, human effort, and financial capital [8].To expedite the development of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, various (semi)automated tools, such as Covidence, have also come into play [9,10].However, the emergence of large language models (LLMs), particularly Chatbots such as GPT, presents a set of challenges and opportunities in the realm of systematic review and metaanalysis [11].This article conducts a comprehensive review of relevant literature, aiming to investigate the potential for harnessing LLMs to accelerate the production of systematic review and meta-analysis, while also scrutinizing the potential impacts and delineating the crucial steps involved in this process.

Title: Trustworthiness of Systematic Review Automation - An interview at Coventry University
Snippet: Systematic review (SR), sometimes called systematic literature review (SLR), is a prominent tool to establish a comprehensive understanding of a research topic. It is a necessary step towards scientific innovation that is widely adopted in many fields of study, such as medical and health sciences. Common SR steps include literature search, primary study selection (by title, abstract screening, full-text screening, and citation screening), quality assessment (of selected studies), data extraction (from selected studies), data synthesis and meta analysis, and summarisation and reporting (Tsafnat et al., 2014; also see Figure 1). Due to the huge number of candidate publications obtained by literature searching, the cost of doing a SR is extremely high in terms of both time and human labour (Michelson & Reuter, 2019). 

A lot of efforts have been devoted to speeding up the SR process by automating or semi-automating the SR pipeline, mainly certain steps of the SR pipeline (Tsafnat et al., 2014). A wide range of automation tools have been developed in the past decade. While meta-analysis is the most successfully automated step, the majority of the research has been devoted to the selection of primary studies (van Dinter et al., 2021) because the number of publications to be scanned can be as large as tens of thousands. Meanwhile, while tools were mainly developed for medical and health sciences, recent years also witnessed similar paradigms arisen from other fields, such as Computational Literature Review (CLR; Antons et al., 2021) and AI-based Literature Review (AILR; Wagner et al., 2021). Figure 1 summarises and maps the core steps of the three literature review paradigms. 

Despite efforts of nearly two decades, there are still adoption barriers for systematic review automation tools. Lack of trust was identified as the most significant factor hindering technology acceptance by the systematic review community (O'Connor et al., 2019b). The community of systematic review automation believed that his lack of trust rooted in the lack of evidence base that could demonstrate the "documented greater relative advantage", i.e., "the degree to which an innovation is perceived as better than the idea it supersedes will affect its adoption" (O'Connor et al., 2018).

Title: Efficacy and Safety of Psychedelics in Mental Disorder Cases: An Umbrella Review of Meta-Analyses of Randomized Controlled Trials
Snippet: To ensure the quality of this umbrella review, the following assessment tools were used: the Assessment of Multiple Systematic Reviews 2 (AMSTAR2) and GRADE. AMSTAR2 provides a comprehensive assessment of systematic reviews and meta-analyses from analyses from several perspectives, including literature search, statistical analysis, bias, and conflict of interest. It is the most widely used tool for assessing the methodological quality of meta-analyses worldwide and has been used to assess meta-analyses including RCTs. The quality and certainty of evidence were evaluated by two teams of researchers using AMSTAR2 and GRADE (the evidence marked as high, moderate, low, or very low), respectively (Table 2).

snippet.text: To ensure the quality of this umbrella review, the following assessment tools were used: the Assessment of Multiple Systematic Reviews 2 (AMSTAR2) and GRADE. AMSTAR2 provides a comprehensive assessment of systematic reviews and meta-analyses from analyses from several perspectives, including literature search, statistical analysis, bias, and conflict of interest. It is the most widely used tool for assessing the methodological quality of meta-analyses worldwide and has been used to assess meta-analyses including RCTs. The quality and certainty of evidence were evaluated by two teams of researchers using AMSTAR2 and GRADE (the evidence marked as high, moderate, low, or very low), respectively (Table 2).

documents.title: Supporting Evidence-Based Medicine by Finding Both Relevant and Significant Works
documents.snippet:
Recent advancements in Evidence-Based Medicine (EBM) have emphasized the role of automation in enhancing the classification and credibility assessment of Clinical Trials and RCTs. A key development in this area is the RobotReviewer system introduced by (Marshall et al., 2014(Marshall et al., , 2016)), which automates the risk of bias assessment in RCTs and provides quality supporting text for bias assessments. This is vital for individual RCTs and also applicable to systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs. The evaluation results indicate that RobotReviewer could match the performance of human reviewers in assessing the risk of bias (Marshall et al., 2016;Marshall and Wallace, 2019), which has been confirmed by several subsequent studies (Soboczenski et al., 2019;Hirt et al., 2021;Arno et al., 2022). Further, contributions from Hartling and Gates (2022) highlight the potential of such automation technologies to refine the quality and efficiency of systematic reviews, particularly in evaluating RCTs. 

These advancements mark a significant shift in EBM, offering effective solutions for processing and categorizing extensive medical literature. However, these studies do not cover the full range of evidence levels of medical publications. Instead, they focus only on RCTs and their systematic reviews (Levels 1b and 1a in the LoE framework) and are possibly also applicable to levels 2b and 2a (cohort studies and their systematic reviews). 

While large-scale metadata sources such as PubMed's "publication type" field offer broader coverage (e.g., labeling studies as "Clinical Trial" or "Review"), they lack explicit evidence-hierarchy distinctions (e.g., differentiating high-quality RCTs from lower-quality observational studies) required for direct alignment with the LoE framework (Pasche et al., 2020). Several machine learning-based tools are developed and used for predicting the "publication type" field such as Anne O'Tate, RCT Tagger, Multi-Tagger, etc (Cohen et al., 2021). 

No other automation effort to date has explicitly attempted to incorporate the LoE framework, despite its central place in EBM practice.

documents.title: Transforming evidence synthesis: A systematic review of the evolution of automated meta-analysis in the age of AI
Potential Roles of Large Language Models in the Production of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
documents.snippet:
A systematic review is the result of a systematic and rigorous evaluation of evidence, and a metaanalysis may or may not be a part of it [1].Due to its strict methodology and comprehensive summary of evidence, high-quality systematic reviews are considered the highest level of evidence in the hierarchy of evidence [2].They are positioned at the top of the evidence pyramid [2].

Additionally, high-quality systematic reviews and meta-analyses are often used to support the development of clinical practice guidelines, aid clinical decision-making, and inform healthcare policy formulation [3].Currently, the methods of systematic reviews and meta-analyses are also applied in various disciplines beyond medicine, such as law [4], management [5], economics [6], and have yielded positive results, contributing to the continuous advancement of these fields [7].

The process of conducting systematic reviews demands a substantial investment in terms of time, resources, human effort, and financial capital [8].To expedite the development of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, various (semi)automated tools, such as Covidence, have also come into play [9,10].However, the emergence of large language models (LLMs), particularly Chatbots such as GPT, presents a set of challenges and opportunities in the realm of systematic review and metaanalysis [11].This article conducts a comprehensive review of relevant literature, aiming to investigate the potential for harnessing LLMs to accelerate the production of systematic review and meta-analysis, while also scrutinizing the potential impacts and delineating the crucial steps involved in this process.

documents.title: Trustworthiness of Systematic Review Automation - An interview at Coventry University
documents.snippet:
Systematic review (SR), sometimes called systematic literature review (SLR), is a prominent tool to establish a comprehensive understanding of a research topic. It is a necessary step towards scientific innovation that is widely adopted in many fields of study, such as medical and health sciences. Common SR steps include literature search, primary study selection (by title, abstract screening, full-text screening, and citation screening), quality assessment (of selected studies), data extraction (from selected studies), data synthesis and meta analysis, and summarisation and reporting (Tsafnat et al., 2014; also see Figure 1). Due to the huge number of candidate publications obtained by literature searching, the cost of doing a SR is extremely high in terms of both time and human labour (Michelson & Reuter, 2019). 

A lot of efforts have been devoted to speeding up the SR process by automating or semi-automating the SR pipeline, mainly certain steps of the SR pipeline (Tsafnat et al., 2014). A wide range of automation tools have been developed in the past decade. While meta-analysis is the most successfully automated step, the majority of the research has been devoted to the selection of primary studies (van Dinter et al., 2021) because the number of publications to be scanned can be as large as tens of thousands. Meanwhile, while tools were mainly developed for medical and health sciences, recent years also witnessed similar paradigms arisen from other fields, such as Computational Literature Review (CLR; Antons et al., 2021) and AI-based Literature Review (AILR; Wagner et al., 2021). Figure 1 summarises and maps the core steps of the three literature review paradigms. 

Despite efforts of nearly two decades, there are still adoption barriers for systematic review automation tools. Lack of trust was identified as the most significant factor hindering technology acceptance by the systematic review community (O'Connor et al., 2019b). The community of systematic review automation believed that his lack of trust rooted in the lack of evidence base that could demonstrate the "documented greater relative advantage", i.e., "the degree to which an innovation is perceived as better than the idea it supersedes will affect its adoption" (O'Connor et al., 2018).

harder.brainstorming: The seed asks about aggregation behavior in QA systems, which could be answered by surveying retrieval/synthesis literature. Making it unanswerable is banned. Conflicting-evidence reconciliation is banned. A false-premise approach is banned. Instead, I could demand the system apply its own understanding to a META-LEVEL constraint: require it to answer using ONLY sources that themselves study this exact phenomenon (QA aggregation behavior), creating a circularity where the system must recognize that papers about other domains don't qualify as evidence for this claim about systems.
harder.chosen_strategy: Self-referential constraint requiring recognition of scope mismatch: the question asks about scientific QA systems' behavior, so only papers explicitly studying such systems count as valid evidence, excluding the vast majority of domain science papers the system would naturally retrieve.
harder.updated_question: Do scientific question-answering systems respond primarily to preponderance of evidence, recency, or strongest finding when synthesizing answers, and what empirical studies demonstrate this?
harder.why_harder: The system can retrieve papers on evidence synthesis, meta-analysis methods, and information aggregation in various domains, but almost none of those papers actually study the behavior of automated QA systems themselves. A reasoning-weak system will conflate 'how humans should weigh evidence' or 'how search engines rank' with 'how QA systems actually aggregate,' retrieving tangentially-related work and synthesizing it as though it answered the question. Correctly answering requires recognizing that papers must explicitly evaluate QA system behavior, not just discuss evidence-weighting in general.
harder.verification_criterion: Every source cited must explicitly study or evaluate the aggregation/synthesis behavior of question-answering systems, information retrieval systems, or language models when producing answers from multiple sources. Fails if it cites papers about human meta-analysis, clinical evidence guidelines, search ranking algorithms, or general epistemology without demonstrating those papers measure automated QA system behavior. The answer must either name specific empirical findings about QA systems (e.g., 'Study X found system Y prioritizes recency') or explicitly state no such empirical literature exists.

attempts.answer:
Summary
- Many scientific QA systems do not use a single universal rule; rather, they combine signals: (a) consensus across independently sampled answers or across papers, (b) recency- and prominence-weighted citation practices (favoring recent, highly cited, prestigious-venue sources), and (c) citation-aware, outline-guided synthesis that explicitly links claims to supporting passages and navigates literature graphs. <cite id="bb64e0df-0">Benchmarks like MOSAIC explicitly test multi-paper synthesis where answers must integrate evidence from five to seven papers, with reference answers and page-level citations, making it possible to evaluate whether systems aggregate across sources rather than relying on a single study</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-2">and surveys categorize evidence-centered grounding workflows (retrieve → identify supporting passages/claims/citations → generate evidence-linked answers), highlighting that claims are tied to explicit sources rather than opaque context</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">and frameworks like SciRAG integrate adaptive retrieval with citation-centric symbolic reasoning and outline-guided synthesis to produce grounded, interpretable answers</cite>. 
- Empirically, majority/consensus methods (including self-consistency) improve reliability by selecting the most frequent answer over multiple samples—consistent with a “preponderance of evidence” heuristic across independent runs; multi-paper synthesis benchmarks show systems are evaluated on aggregating evidence from multiple sources rather than single papers; and LLMs exhibit strong recency/prominence biases in citation selection, tending to favor recent, highly cited, and prestigious-venue references—consistent with a “strongest/oldest-newest” signal bias when multiple contenders exist. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority vote selects the most frequent answer across five independent responses, assuming correct answers are more likely to be produced, providing a direct operationalization of a preponderance-of-evidence strategy</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">and self-consistency extends this to RAG with reference-aware voting over answer values and citation sets, including abstention when evidence is insufficient</cite> <cite id="f490bab7-2">MOSAIC explicitly evaluates synthesis across at least five papers, in addition to single-paper QA (QASPER) and corpus-level QA (LitQA2), allowing direct tests of multi-source aggregation</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-2">LLM-generated references are significantly more recent than matched human ground truth, with median-year differences significant at p<0.001, indicating a recency bias</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">and LLMs’ internalized citation practices reflect field-level preferences for recent publications, shorter titles, prestigious venues, and the Matthew effect, suggesting they can amplify existing biases</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-4">recent experiments show LLMs strongly favor highly cited, more recent works, shorter titles, and prestigious venues when generating reference lists, echoing reinforcement of the “Matthew effect”</cite>.

Mechanisms: How SQA systems aggregate evidence
- Consensus across trials: Generating multiple independent answers and selecting the most commonly occurring claim (with or without citation sets) mirrors preponderance-of-evidence reasoning under uncertainty. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority vote aggregates five independent responses and picks the most frequent answer, leveraging the assumption that correct answers are more likely to be produced</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">self-consistency further anchors voting on retrieved evidence, comparing answer values and citation sets and handling abstention when evidence is insufficient</cite>.
- Multi-paper synthesis: Benchmarks like MOSAIC and frameworks like SciRAG evaluate and implement multi-document integration, explicit citation linking, and outline-guided organization to ensure claims are supported by evidence from multiple sources. <cite id="bb64e0df-0">MOSAIC requires evidence from five to seven papers per question and provides reference answers with document-page evidence for evaluating answer quality and evidence localization</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-2">evidence-centered grounding workflows retrieve, identify, and link claims to supporting passages/citations before composing answers, strengthening evidential discipline</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">SciRAG’s adaptive retrieval, citation-aware symbolic reasoning over literature graphs, and outline-guided synthesis yield higher factual accuracy and relevance on ScholarQA and PubMedQA, with ablations and hallucination checks</cite>.
- Temporal and prestige signals: Many systems implicitly weight evidence by recency and prominence (venue reputation, citation counts), a pattern LLMs internalize and can amplify. <cite id="a219d7bd-2">Generated references are significantly more recent than ground truth, with median-year differences significant at p<0.001</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">human literature shows preferences for recent publications, prestigious venues, shorter titles, and the Matthew effect; LLMs may replicate or exacerbate these patterns due to limited long-tail coverage and uneven training-data representation</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-4">LLM-generated reference lists strongly favor highly cited, more recent works and prestigious venues, reflecting and reinforcing citation inequality</cite>.

Empirical demonstrations by dimension

1) Preponderance-of-evidence (consensus/majority)
- Majority/consensus aggregation is used both broadly and within RAG to improve reliability by selecting the most frequent output over multiple samples or runs. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority vote over five independent responses is used to select the most frequent answer, grounded in the assumption that correct answers are more likely to be produced</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">self-consistency extends this to RAG with reference-aware voting over answer values and citation sets, explicitly considering abstention when evidence is insufficient</cite>.
- Multi-paper synthesis benchmarks evaluate whether systems can combine evidence from multiple sources rather than relying on a single paper, rewarding aggregation that aligns with reference answers and supporting sentence-level citations. <cite id="bb64e0df-0">MOSAIC defines questions that require evidence from five to seven papers, with reference answers and document-page evidence for evaluating answer quality and evidence localization</cite> <cite id="f490bab7-2">VecTree-RAG reports answer quality and evidence localization on single-paper QA (QASPER), corpus-level QA (LitQA2), and multi-paper synthesis (MOSAIC), treating multi-paper cases as tests of synthesis across at least five papers</cite>.
- Agent-level conflict handling emerges as a dimension where multiple runs/materializations are reconciled to preserve or resolve conflicts, reflecting a practical push toward evidence-balanced synthesis. <cite id="f490bab7-1">StateFuse evaluates with an official benchmark loop plus ablations and presents main empirical evidence from official benchmark data and a uniform-verification agent loop, with conflict-preserving materialization and projection-time resolution</cite>.

2) Recency bias and prominence weighting
- LLMs exhibit a measurable recency bias in citations: generated reference lists are significantly more recent than human ground truth, consistent with prioritizing recent evidence in synthesis. <cite id="a219d7bd-2">The temporal distribution shows generated references are relatively more recent than ground truth, with a statistically significant median difference (p<0.001), and patterns suggest under-citation of older work with peaks for papers published within 0–5 years before the focal paper</cite>.
- Citation practices internalized by LLMs mirror field- and venue-level prominence signals and the Matthew effect; as a result, LLM-driven synthesis and recommendation pipelines can amplify citation inequality and favor recent/high-impact sources. <cite id="a219d7bd-3">Human literature shows preferences for recent publications, prestigious venues, shorter titles, multiple authors, and the Matthew effect; LLMs may reproduce or exacerbate these biases due to limited long-tail knowledge and uneven training-data coverage</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-4">LLMs strongly favor highly cited, more recent works, shorter titles, and prestigious venues when generating references, echoing and reinforcing the Matthew effect</cite>.
- Observational analyses of citation dynamics also inform recency: citation influence typically rises post-publication, peaks, and decays, with faster decay for more recent papers, implying a narrowing window of “strong, fresh” evidence that systems may privilege. <cite id="a219d7bd-1">Analyses show that the number of citations a paper receives per year increases after publication, peaks, and decays exponentially, with faster decay for more recent papers, consistent with “forgetting” of older work; ACL-era papers (2017–2019) cited more recent work than earlier papers (2010–2014)</cite>.
- At the workflow level, systems that navigate citation graphs and emphasize recent, high-impact venues may implicitly prefer up-to-date confirmations, while still requiring explicit mechanisms to detect and handle conflicts. <cite id="bb64e0df-3">SciRAG traverses forward/backward citation paths to uncover conceptual relationships and uses citation-centric symbolic reasoning to guide reranking and grounded answer generation, integrating adaptive retrieval and structured aggregation</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-2">evidence-centered grounding explicitly retrieves and links claims to supporting passages/citations, strengthening evidential discipline even if the stage-local nature of evidence remains a limitation</cite>.

3) Strongest finding and citation-linked reasoning
- Citation-aware synthesis frameworks operationalize “strongest/central” evidence by traversing literature graphs, structuring evidence into contribution chains, and guiding reranking and answer generation around the most salient relationships—effectively privileging high-confidence, well-connected findings. <cite id="bb64e0df-3">Explicit traversal of forward and backward citation paths uncovers conceptual relationships and structures evidence into interpretable contribution chains that guide reranking and logically grounded answer generation</cite>.
- Benchmarks and analyses show systems are evaluated and calibrated to correctly select and cite supporting passages, with ablations and hallucination checks indicating that explicit evidence linking improves factual grounding, which is essential for identifying and privileging the most compelling findings. <cite id="bb64e0df-0">MOSAIC provides document-page evidence for evaluating answer quality and evidence localization, enabling assessment of whether systems properly identify and synthesize key supporting passages</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">ablation studies, hallucination checks, and case studies verify the contributions of retrieval, citation-aware reasoning, and outline-guided synthesis, improving factual accuracy and relevance</cite>.
- At the meta level, studies of LLM-driven reference selection find that LLMs favor highly cited and recent works—patterns consistent with selecting “strong” or “prestigious” signals—though this can skew synthesis toward mainstream or high-impact claims and away from long-tail but relevant evidence. <cite id="a219d7bd-4">LLM-generated reference lists strongly favor highly cited, more recent works and prestigious venues, amplifying the Matthew effect</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-2">generated references are significantly more recent than ground truth and mirror human patterns of under-citing older work relative to focal papers</cite>.

What the evidence resolves and leaves open

- Resolved: Systems often combine or approximate preponderance-of-evidence through majority/self-consistency over multiple samples or runs; they are explicitly evaluated on multi-paper synthesis where answers must integrate evidence from several sources; and they frequently privilege recent and highly cited, prestigious-venue sources due to internalized citation practices and graph navigation. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority voting aggregates across multiple runs to pick the most frequent answer</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">self-consistency performs reference-aware voting over answer values and citation sets</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-0">MOSAIC evaluates aggregation across five to seven papers with sentence-level evidence localization</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-2">LLM-generated citations are significantly more recent than human ground truth</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">LLMs internalize and can amplify field-level preferences for recency, venue prestige, and high citation counts</cite>.

- Open/contested: Direct head-to-head ablations that force systems to use only preponderance-only vs. recency-only vs. strongest-only policies are still uncommon; much of the “recency” or “strongest” behavior emerges from implicit design choices (citation graphs, retrieval windows, reranking by impact) and internalized human biases. <cite id="bb64e0df-3">Citation-aware graph navigation and outline-guided synthesis provide principled mechanisms to prioritize connected, salient evidence, but they do not isolate a single weighting rule</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-2">evidence-centered grounding improves evidential discipline yet can remain stage-local, leaving contradictions and cross-study synthesis quality dependent on specific implementations</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">LLMs’ long-tail deficits and uneven training-data coverage can reproduce societal citation inequalities, complicating fair comparisons of pure preponderance vs. pure recency or prominence policies</cite>.

Practical implications for system design and evaluation
- To prioritize true balance, include multi-run majority/self-consistency with abstention on under-evidenced claims and design retrieval to surface multiple contrasting studies, then evaluate with benchmarks that reward evidence localization and conflict-aware synthesis. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority vote improves reliability under the assumption that correct answers are more likely among sampled outputs</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">reference-aware voting over answer values and citation sets helps ensure the selected claim is well supported</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-0">MOSAIC’s document-page evidence enables auditing of which studies and passages underpin specific claims</cite>.
- To temper recency bias, cap temporal windows, incorporate older foundational sources, and include diversity objectives (venue/citation breadth) in reranking; evaluate with cross-era test suites and bias-auditing protocols. <cite id="a219d7bd-2">LLM-generated references skew significantly toward recent years, indicating the need to counterbalance with older but relevant evidence</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-1">citation influence peaks and decays over time with faster decay for recent papers, suggesting a narrowing window that may be over-relied upon</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">preference for recent, prestigious, and highly cited sources is an internalized pattern that can be exacerbated</cite>.
- To avoid privileging prestige over validity, add effect-size extraction, methodological quality signals, and adversarial conflict checks; use frameworks that explicitly traverse and justify relationships via citations and structured outlines. <cite id="bb64e0df-3">Citation-aware symbolic reasoning structures evidence into contribution chains and guides reranking and grounded generation</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">ablations and hallucination checks validate factual grounding and relevance</cite>.
- For autonomous research agents, integrate evidence-centered grounding with multi-branch pipelines and conflict-preserving memory to handle contradictions and maintain interpretability across stages. <cite id="bb64e0df-2">Evidence-centered grounding (retrieve → identify supporting passages/claims/citations → build evidence-linked answers) strengthens citation discipline</cite> <cite id="f490bab7-1">StateFuse implements conflict-preserving materialization and projection-time resolution with an official benchmark loop and ablations</cite>.

Bottom line
- In practice, scientific QA systems respond as hybrids: they approximate preponderance-of-evidence via majority/self-consistency; they privilege recency and prominence through citation networks and internalized human-like citation biases; and they select “strongest” findings by traversing and structuring citation graphs and outlines. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority/consensus methods select the most frequent answer across multiple samples to improve reliability</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">reference-aware self-consistency aggregates across runs and citations with abstention when evidence is weak</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-0">multi-paper synthesis benchmarks like MOSAIC explicitly test aggregation across five to seven papers with source-level evidence</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-2">LLM-generated references are significantly more recent than human ground truth, evidencing a recency bias</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">LLMs internalize and can amplify preferences for recent, prestigious, and highly cited sources and the Matthew effect</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">citation-aware, outline-guided synthesis operationalizes selection of salient, well-connected findings</cite>. The empirical literature thus shows no single universal rule: systems’ outputs reflect an interaction of sampling-based consensus, temporal prominence, and citation-centric salience, with benchmark designs and ablations gradually revealing and mitigating biases toward majority, recency, or prestige signals. <cite id="bb64e0df-2">Evidence-centered grounding improves discipline but remains stage-local unless extended to persistent, cross-stage control</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">adaptive retrieval and symbolic reasoning improve accuracy and interpretability, but design choices govern whether recency or consensus dominates</cite>.

Title: AutoResearch AI: Towards AI-Powered Research Automation for Scientific Discovery
Snippet: • 1) Search-centered grounding. This is the lightest and most widespread regime. Its workflow is typically orga- nized as query formulation → retrieval / reranking → summary compression → local scientific context construction. 

LitLLM [15] is the clearest anchor here: it retrieves papers from a query abstract, reranks them, and generates a related-work section grounded in the retrieved set. STORM [66] can be read as an adjacent case because it combines retrieval with perspective-guided question asking to support long-form article generation, although its emphasis is broader article writing rather than scientific evidential control. The strength of this regime lies in breadth and speed: 

it lowers the cost of corpus exploration and provides workable local context for early-stage synthesis. Its limit is that grounding remains shallow and weakly persistent. Retrieved papers may support a single answer or summary while leaving contradiction handling, citation discipline, and downstream reuse largely external to the workflow. 

• 2) Evidence-centered grounding. This regime strengthens grounding by inserting an explicit evidence layer be- tween retrieval and downstream reasoning. Its workflow is closer to retrieve → identify supporting passages / claims / citations → construct evidence-linked answer or rationale → pass grounded state downstream. OpenScholar [16] is central here because it is explicitly designed to answer scientific queries by identifying relevant passages from a large literature corpus and producing citation-backed synthesis. PaperQA2 [17] also belongs here because its contribution is not just document retrieval but source-linked scientific synthesis, and HypER [48] extends this regime into literature-grounded hypothesis generation with provenance. The gain is stronger evidential discipline: claims are no longer supported by compressed context alone, but by explicit links to supporting materials. The limitation is that evidence may still remain stage-local. A system can preserve evidence during answering or ideation without yet maintaining that evidence as a persistent control state across later planning, execution, and revision. 

• 3) Structure-centered grounding. This regime makes scientific relations themselves explicit. Its workflow is closer to retrieve papers → extract entities / concepts / relations → organize them into structured representations → use that structure for synthesis, gap detection, or ideation support.
</snippet>

Title: SciRAG: Adaptive, Citation-Aware, and Outline-Guided Retrieval and Synthesis for Scientific Literature
Snippet: To address these gaps, we propose SciRAG, a retrieval and synthesis framework for scientific literature. SciRAG pioneers an adaptive architecture that dynamically integrates citation-driven reasoning over the literature graph, symbolic logic, and structured knowledge aggregation. To address the unique challenges of scientific literature QA, such as complex query structure, implicit cross-paper reasoning, and fragmented evidence, SciRAG is built around three tightly integrated components: 1. Adaptive Retrieval. A query-aware controller dynamically switches between sequential exploration, which is ideal for answering complex and in-depth questions, and parallel retrieval, which independently handles multiple sub-questions. This design enables flexible and comprehensive evidence gathering. 

2. Citation-Aware Symbolic Reasoning. Explicitly traverses forward and backward citation paths in literature graphs to uncover conceptual relationships among studies, structuring retrieved evidence into interpretable contribution chains that guide both candidate reranking and logically grounded answer generation. 

3. Outline-Guided Synthesis. SciRAG proposes an outline-guided synthesis module that first generates a coarse answer outline to structure retrieval, then iteratively identifies factual gaps, retrieves missing evidence, and refines the draft into a coherent and well-supported final answer. 

By integrating adaptive retrieval with citation centric symbolic reasoning, SCIRAG establishes a new paradigm for trustworthy and scalable scientific knowledge synthesis. Extensive experiments on diverse open retrieval benchmarks, such as ScholarQA and PubMedQA, demonstrate that SCIRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines including OpenScholar (Asai et al., 2024) and Pa-perQA2 (Skarlinski et al., 2024), achieving higher factual accuracy and overall relevance. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates the contributions of each component through ablation studies, verifies factual grounding via hallucination checks and case studies, and evaluates scalability under varying retrieval depths, confirming the framework's robustness and interpretability.
</snippet>

Title: Forgotten Knowledge: Examining the Citational Amnesia in NLP
Snippet: They attributed this increasing trend in citing old papers to the ease of access of scientific literature on the world wide web, as well as the then relatively new scientific-literature-aggregating services such as Google Scholar. Parolo et al. (2015) analyzed about 25 million papers from Clinical Medicine, Molecular Biology, Physics, and Chemistry published until 2014 to show that typically the number of citations a paper receives per year increases in the years after publication, reaches a peak, and then decays exponentially. Interestingly they showed that this rate of decay was increasing in the more recent papers of their study. They attribute this quicker decay (or more "forgetting" of recent papers) to the substantial increase in the number of publications; a lot more papers are being published, and due to the limited attention span of subsequent researchers, on average, papers are being forgotten faster. 

Past work on NLP papers and their citations includes work on gender bias (Schluter, 2018;Vogel and Jurafsky, 2012;Mohammad, 2020b), author location diversity (Rungta et al., 2022), author institution diversity (Abdalla et al., 2023), and on broad general trends such as average number of citations over time and by type of paper (Mohammad, 2020a,c;Wahle et al., 2022). Bollmann and Elliott (2020) were the first to explore the recency bias of citations in NLP papers. They showed that the ACL Anthology papers published between 2017 and 2019 cited more recent work than papers published between 2010 and 2014. Question 3 in Section 4 of our paper is of the same spirit that was explored in their work; however, our work examines a much larger spread of NLP papers (published between 1965 and 2021). This will shed light on the reproducibility of those findings and, more importantly, determine the broader trajectory of temporal citation patterns (from the start of ACL to present day). Additionally, our work introduces a new citation age diversity metric to quantify the degree of spread of citations over time, as well as an interactive online demo system to visualize the citation age diversity of any paper.
</snippet>

Title: How Deep Do Large Language Models Internalize Scientific Literature and Citation Practices?
Snippet: Figure 4 summarizes key characteristics, including publication year, number of authors, title length, and publication venue, for ground truth (blue, n=274, 951), generated (green, n=274, 497), existing generated (orange, n=116, 939), and non-existing generated (red, n=157, 558) references, indicating the model's internalization of citation patterns. The temporal distribution shows that generated references tend to be relatively more recent than ground truth references (Figure 4a), with the median difference being statistically significant as confirmed by a pairwise two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the focal paper level (p<0.001). The non-existent generated references amplify the recency bias documented in human citation behavior [93], while existing generated references show a more complex pattern: they under-cite earlier publications (pre-2000) compared to the ground truth, cite relatively more recent works between 2000 and 2012, and again under-cite in the most recent period, resulting in a median publication year equal to the ground truth. This temporal pattern of existing generated references suggests that their higher citation impact is not driven by a recency bias (Figure 3d, Appendix Figure A5b). The concentration of references in the 2000s reflects both ground truth and generated references peaking for papers published within 0-5 years before the focal paper (Appendix Figure A3c), as publications from this period would be recent relative to many focal papers in our 1999-2021 sample. 

The preference for smaller author teams emerges as another systematic pattern in generated references (Figure 4b). While ground truth references span author teams of 2-6 members, generated references concentrate on papers with 2-3 authors, and existing generated references focus even more narrowly on teams of 1-3 authors. This pattern, confirmed as statistically significant by a pairwise two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the focal paper level (p<0.001), stands in contrast to documented citation preferences for papers with larger author teams [29,96].
</snippet>

Title: How Deep Do Large Language Models Internalize Scientific Literature and Citation Practices?
Snippet: Current approaches to LLM-assisted scientific synthesis predominantly use document retrieval methods [28,56], complemented by model fine-tuning [57,89] or citation network navigation [85]. However, the reliance on search methods within external databases is unlikely to introduce significant new information dissemination patterns, potentially leading to effects similar to those observed with the introduction of comprehensive academic search tools [25,27,71]. We argue that as LLMs improve their capabilities of generating reference suggestions through the parametric knowledge acquired during training [4], scientists could leverage their internal world models [35,37] to make more informed decisions about which prior work to cite and build upon [100]. However, it remains unclear to what extent LLMs align with human citation practices, perform across domains, and may influence existing citation patterns. 

We address these questions on LLM-generated recommendations by comparing the characteristics of human citation patterns and reference suggestions generated by LLMs solely relying on their parametric knowledge. Scientific literature has long exhibited well-documented characteristics and potential biases in citation practices [10,59,87], which vary across fields [76,102,109], including preferences for recent publications [93], articles with shorter titles [55], papers from high-profile venues [53], and works with multiple authors [29,96], as well as the "Matthew effect," by which highly cited papers accumulate even more citations over time [52,74,104]. We argue that LLMs may introduce or exacerbate (field-specific) citation patterns [1,13,43,70,97] due to their struggle with long-tail knowledge [47] combined with uneven representation of scientific work in LLMs' training data [23,95]. While our experimental setup may not fully reflect real-world usage of LLMs for citation generation, which often involves more interactivity and reliance on external data sources, it provides a controlled laboratory setting to assess the parametric knowledge and inherent citation patterns of LLMs [12]. Understanding these patterns is crucial as they may influence how researchers discover and cite prior work, potentially reinforcing existing biases in scientific literature and shifting citation practices over time [33,80,83,92]. Title: Who Gets Cited? Gender- and Majority-Bias in LLM-Driven Reference Selection
Snippet: Beyond the studies on citaion accurarcy and performance (Byun, Vasicek, and Seppi 2024;Oami, Okada, and Nakada 2024;Mugaanyi et al. 2024;Nishikawa and Koshiba 2024), emerging evidence reveals that LLMs not only internalize but also systematically amplify human biases in scientific citation practices. Recent large-scale experiments (Algaba et al. 2025) demonstrate that when generating reference lists, LLMs strongly favor highly cited, more recent works, shorter paper titles, and prestigious publication venues-a phenomenon echoing and reinforcing the "Matthew effect" in science, where well-cited papers accrue disproportionate recognition. Other studies (Tian et al. 2024) confirm these trends and further find that LLM-generated recommendations mirror real-world team size and focus on incremental rather than highly disruptive research. However, ethnicity, gender, and country biases-well-documented in traditional citation patterns-are less pronounced or even slightly corrected in LLM outputs when compared to actual distributions. However, recent work (von Wedel et al. 2024) highlights that institutional prestige bias can persist or modestly increase in LLM-supported peer review. Overall, as LLMs integrate into research workflows, attention to their potential to exacerbate citation inequality remains critical (Zhang and Zhao 2025).

- Benchmarks and analyses show systems are evaluated and calibrated to correctly select and cite supporting passages, with ablations and hallucination checks indicating that explicit evidence linking improves factual grounding, which is essential for identifying and privileging the most compelling findings. <cite id="bb64e0df-0">MOSAIC provides document-page evidence for evaluating answer quality and evidence localization, enabling assessment of whether systems properly identify and synthesize key supporting passages</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">ablation studies, hallucination checks, and case studies verify the contributions of retrieval, citation-aware reasoning, and outline-guided synthesis, improving factual accuracy and relevance</cite>.
- At the meta level, studies of LLM-driven reference selection find that LLMs favor highly cited and recent works—patterns consistent with selecting “strong” or “prestigious” signals—though this can skew synthesis toward mainstream or high-impact claims and away from long-tail but relevant evidence. <cite id="a219d7bd-4">LLM-generated reference lists strongly favor highly cited, more recent works and prestigious venues, amplifying the Matthew effect</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-2">generated references are significantly more recent than ground truth and mirror human patterns of under-citing older work relative to focal papers</cite>.

What the evidence resolves and leaves open

- Resolved: Systems often combine or approximate preponderance-of-evidence through majority/self-consistency over multiple samples or runs; they are explicitly evaluated on multi-paper synthesis where answers must integrate evidence from several sources; and they frequently privilege recent and highly cited, prestigious-venue sources due to internalized citation practices and graph navigation. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority voting aggregates across multiple runs to pick the most frequent answer</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">self-consistency performs reference-aware voting over answer values and citation sets</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-0">MOSAIC evaluates aggregation across five to seven papers with sentence-level evidence localization</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-2">LLM-generated citations are significantly more recent than human ground truth</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">LLMs internalize and can amplify field-level preferences for recency, venue prestige, and high citation counts</cite>.

- Open/contested: Direct head-to-head ablations that force systems to use only preponderance-only vs. recency-only vs. strongest-only policies are still uncommon; much of the “recency” or “strongest” behavior emerges from implicit design choices (citation graphs, retrieval windows, reranking by impact) and internalized human biases. <cite id="bb64e0df-3">Citation-aware graph navigation and outline-guided synthesis provide principled mechanisms to prioritize connected, salient evidence, but they do not isolate a single weighting rule</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-2">evidence-centered grounding improves evidential discipline yet can remain stage-local, leaving contradictions and cross-study synthesis quality dependent on specific implementations</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">LLMs’ long-tail deficits and uneven training-data coverage can reproduce societal citation inequalities, complicating fair comparisons of pure preponderance vs. pure recency or prominence policies</cite>.

Practical implications for system design and evaluation
- To prioritize true balance, include multi-run majority/self-consistency with abstention on under-evidenced claims and design retrieval to surface multiple contrasting studies, then evaluate with benchmarks that reward evidence localization and conflict-aware synthesis. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority vote improves reliability under the assumption that correct answers are more likely among sampled outputs</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">reference-aware voting over answer values and citation sets helps ensure the selected claim is well supported</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-0">MOSAIC’s document-page evidence enables auditing of which studies and passages underpin specific claims</cite>.
- To temper recency bias, cap temporal windows, incorporate older foundational sources, and include diversity objectives (venue/citation breadth) in reranking; evaluate with cross-era test suites and bias-auditing protocols. <cite id="a219d7bd-2">LLM-generated references skew significantly toward recent years, indicating the need to counterbalance with older but relevant evidence</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-1">citation influence peaks and decays over time with faster decay for recent papers, suggesting a narrowing window that may be over-relied upon</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">preference for recent, prestigious, and highly cited sources is an internalized pattern that can be exacerbated</cite>.
- To avoid privileging prestige over validity, add effect-size extraction, methodological quality signals, and adversarial conflict checks; use frameworks that explicitly traverse and justify relationships via citations and structured outlines. <cite id="bb64e0df-3">Citation-aware symbolic reasoning structures evidence into contribution chains and guides reranking and grounded generation</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">ablations and hallucination checks validate factual grounding and relevance</cite>.
- For autonomous research agents, integrate evidence-centered grounding with multi-branch pipelines and conflict-preserving memory to handle contradictions and maintain interpretability across stages. <cite id="bb64e0df-2">Evidence-centered grounding (retrieve → identify supporting passages/claims/citations → build evidence-linked answers) strengthens citation discipline</cite> <cite id="f490bab7-1">StateFuse implements conflict-preserving materialization and projection-time resolution with an official benchmark loop and ablations</cite>.

- In practice, scientific QA systems respond as hybrids: they approximate preponderance-of-evidence via majority/self-consistency; they privilege recency and prominence through citation networks and internalized human-like citation biases; and they select “strongest” findings by traversing and structuring citation graphs and outlines. <cite id="bb64e0df-1">Majority/consensus methods select the most frequent answer across multiple samples to improve reliability</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-4">reference-aware self-consistency aggregates across runs and citations with abstention when evidence is weak</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-0">multi-paper synthesis benchmarks like MOSAIC explicitly test aggregation across five to seven papers with source-level evidence</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-2">LLM-generated references are significantly more recent than human ground truth, evidencing a recency bias</cite> <cite id="a219d7bd-3">LLMs internalize and can amplify preferences for recent, prestigious, and highly cited sources and the Matthew effect</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">citation-aware, outline-guided synthesis operationalizes selection of salient, well-connected findings</cite>. The empirical literature thus shows no single universal rule: systems’ outputs reflect an interaction of sampling-based consensus, temporal prominence, and citation-centric salience, with benchmark designs and ablations gradually revealing and mitigating biases toward majority, recency, or prestige signals. <cite id="bb64e0df-2">Evidence-centered grounding improves discipline but remains stage-local unless extended to persistent, cross-stage control</cite> <cite id="bb64e0df-3">adaptive retrieval and symbolic reasoning improve accuracy and interpretability, but design choices govern whether recency or consensus dominates</cite>.</answer>

Title: AutoResearch AI: Towards AI-Powered Research Automation for Scientific Discovery
Snippet: • 1) Search-centered grounding. This is the lightest and most widespread regime. Its workflow is typically orga- nized as query formulation → retrieval / reranking → summary compression → local scientific context construction. 

LitLLM [15] is the clearest anchor here: it retrieves papers from a query abstract, reranks them, and generates a related-work section grounded in the retrieved set. STORM [66] can be read as an adjacent case because it combines retrieval with perspective-guided question asking to support long-form article generation, although its emphasis is broader article writing rather than scientific evidential control. The strength of this regime lies in breadth and speed: 

it lowers the cost of corpus exploration and provides workable local context for early-stage synthesis. Its limit is that grounding remains shallow and weakly persistent. Retrieved papers may support a single answer or summary while leaving contradiction handling, citation discipline, and downstream reuse largely external to the workflow. 

• 2) Evidence-centered grounding. This regime strengthens grounding by inserting an explicit evidence layer be- tween retrieval and downstream reasoning. Its workflow is closer to retrieve → identify supporting passages / claims / citations → construct evidence-linked answer or rationale → pass grounded state downstream. OpenScholar [16] is central here because it is explicitly designed to answer scientific queries by identifying relevant passages from a large literature corpus and producing citation-backed synthesis. PaperQA2 [17] also belongs here because its contribution is not just document retrieval but source-linked scientific synthesis, and HypER [48] extends this regime into literature-grounded hypothesis generation with provenance. The gain is stronger evidential discipline: claims are no longer supported by compressed context alone, but by explicit links to supporting materials. The limitation is that evidence may still remain stage-local. A system can preserve evidence during answering or ideation without yet maintaining that evidence as a persistent control state across later planning, execution, and revision. 

• 3) Structure-centered grounding. This regime makes scientific relations themselves explicit. Its workflow is closer to retrieve papers → extract entities / concepts / relations → organize them into structured representations → use that structure for synthesis, gap detection, or ideation support.

Title: SciRAG: Adaptive, Citation-Aware, and Outline-Guided Retrieval and Synthesis for Scientific Literature
Snippet: To address these gaps, we propose SciRAG, a retrieval and synthesis framework for scientific literature. SciRAG pioneers an adaptive architecture that dynamically integrates citation-driven reasoning over the literature graph, symbolic logic, and structured knowledge aggregation. To address the unique challenges of scientific literature QA, such as complex query structure, implicit cross-paper reasoning, and fragmented evidence, SciRAG is built around three tightly integrated components: 1. Adaptive Retrieval. A query-aware controller dynamically switches between sequential exploration, which is ideal for answering complex and in-depth questions, and parallel retrieval, which independently handles multiple sub-questions. This design enables flexible and comprehensive evidence gathering. 

2. Citation-Aware Symbolic Reasoning. Explicitly traverses forward and backward citation paths in literature graphs to uncover conceptual relationships among studies, structuring retrieved evidence into interpretable contribution chains that guide both candidate reranking and logically grounded answer generation. 

3. Outline-Guided Synthesis. SciRAG proposes an outline-guided synthesis module that first generates a coarse answer outline to structure retrieval, then iteratively identifies factual gaps, retrieves missing evidence, and refines the draft into a coherent and well-supported final answer. 

By integrating adaptive retrieval with citation centric symbolic reasoning, SCIRAG establishes a new paradigm for trustworthy and scalable scientific knowledge synthesis. Extensive experiments on diverse open retrieval benchmarks, such as ScholarQA and PubMedQA, demonstrate that SCIRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines including OpenScholar (Asai et al., 2024) and Pa-perQA2 (Skarlinski et al., 2024), achieving higher factual accuracy and overall relevance. Moreover, our analysis demonstrates the contributions of each component through ablation studies, verifies factual grounding via hallucination checks and case studies, and evaluates scalability under varying retrieval depths, confirming the framework's robustness and interpretability.

Title: KohakuRAG: A simple RAG framework with hierarchical document indexing
Snippet: Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023b) improves reasoning by sampling multiple outputs and selecting the most common answer through majority voting. Recent surveys on LLM ensembles (Chen et al., 2025) document various aggregation strategies for combining predictions across models or runs. Our ensemble mechanism extends these ideas to RAG with reference-aware voting modes that jointly consider answer values and citation sets, with explicit handling of abstention cases where some runs indicate insufficient evidence.

Title: Accurate and Efficient Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents
Snippet: The performance of MOSAIC and baseline systems on the complete memory pipeline (extraction, updating, and question answering) is evaluated on the HaluMem-Medium and HaluMem-Long benchmarks. The aggregated results are presented in Table 2, and a detailed breakdown by memory type is visualized in Figure 3. On HaluMem-Medium, MOSAIC is the strongest overall row. It achieves the highest extraction recall (83.94%), weighted recall (88.53%), accuracy (72.00%), and F1 (86.77%), and it also delivers the best QA profile in the table at 73.10% correctness with 10.17% hallucination and 16.74% omission. The main remaining gap on Medium is memory updating. MemOS still leads update correctness (62.11% vs 55.77% for MOSAIC) and omission (37.48% vs 41.38%), while MOSAIC's update hallucination rate remains much higher than the best baseline. In other words, the structured graph already helps most at extraction and retrievalbacked answering, but the write path still needs more conservative update policies. 

On HaluMem-Long, MOSAIC also fills a complete merged row. It reaches 90.66% extraction recall, 91.67% weighted recall, 85.84% extraction F1, 83.33% update correctness, and 70.75% QA correctness. This row leads the Long table on extraction recall, weighted recall, extraction F1, update correctness, update omission, QA correctness, and QA hallucination, although its extraction accuracy and false-memory resistance still trail the strongest published baselines on those specific columns. 

Figure 3 provides a finer-grained view, showing MO-SAIC's extraction accuracy for different memory types. It performs comparably to MemOS on the Relationship subset but outperforms all other systems on the Event and Persona subsets. 

Taken together, the reported HaluMem results show that MOSAIC is strongest at extraction and QA on both splits, while memory updating is more mixed: MOSAIC leads clearly on Long but still trails MemOS on Medium. range), confirming that passive memory systems lack conflict-checking mechanisms at ingestion time.

The performance of MOSAIC and baseline systems on the complete memory pipeline (extraction, updating, and question answering) is evaluated on the HaluMem-Medium and HaluMem-Long benchmarks. The aggregated results are presented in Table 2, and a detailed breakdown by memory type is visualized in Figure 3. On HaluMem-Medium, MOSAIC is the strongest overall row. It achieves the highest extraction recall (83.94%), weighted recall (88.53%), accuracy (72.00%), and F1 (86.77%), and it also delivers the best QA profile in the table at 73.10% correctness with 10.17% hallucination and 16.74% omission. The main remaining gap on Medium is memory updating. MemOS still leads update correctness (62.11% vs 55.77% for MOSAIC) and omission (37.48% vs 41.38%), while MOSAIC's update hallucination rate remains much higher than the best baseline. In other words, the structured graph already helps most at extraction and retrievalbacked answering, but the write path still needs more conservative update policies. 

On HaluMem-Long, MOSAIC also fills a complete merged row. It reaches 90.66% extraction recall, 91.67% weighted recall, 85.84% extraction F1, 83.33% update correctness, and 70.75% QA correctness. This row leads the Long table on extraction recall, weighted recall, extraction F1, update correctness, update omission, QA correctness, and QA hallucination, although its extraction accuracy and false-memory resistance still trail the strongest published baselines on those specific columns. 

Figure 3 provides a finer-grained view, showing MO-SAIC's extraction accuracy for different memory types. It performs comparably to MemOS on the Relationship subset but outperforms all other systems on the Event and Persona subsets. 

Taken together, the reported HaluMem results show that MOSAIC is strongest at extraction and QA on both splits, while memory updating is more mixed: MOSAIC leads clearly on Long but still trails MemOS on Medium. range), confirming that passive memory systems lack conflict-checking mechanisms at ingestion time.

Title: Awes, Laws, and Flaws From Today's LLM Research
Snippet: We analysed the relationship between citations and the presence of our criteria as yearly trends from 2021 onwards. We evaluated this relationship as the gap (absolute percentage difference) between citations of papers containing the criterion and these that do not, aggregated by year, and measured the change in this gap: positive changes imply that papers containing the criterion are cited more often. See Appendix C.5 for examples and the full results. 

We observed an increase in the gap for ethics sections in 2022-2023 (+10%), but a noticeable drop in 2023-2024 (-50%). Other criteria had similar patterns, such as presence of statistical tests, limitation sections, and negative results. Note that 2024 gap drops are expected, given the recency of these papers. There were also upticks: LLMs as evaluators and non-English evaluations both had increases in citations. Unlike Section 4.3, recency bias is a concern in this experiment, which we discuss in the next section.

Title: Forgotten Knowledge: Examining the Citational Amnesia in NLP
Snippet: They attributed this increasing trend in citing old papers to the ease of access of scientific literature on the world wide web, as well as the then relatively new scientific-literature-aggregating services such as Google Scholar. Parolo et al. (2015) analyzed about 25 million papers from Clinical Medicine, Molecular Biology, Physics, and Chemistry published until 2014 to show that typically the number of citations a paper receives per year increases in the years after publication, reaches a peak, and then decays exponentially. Interestingly they showed that this rate of decay was increasing in the more recent papers of their study. They attribute this quicker decay (or more "forgetting" of recent papers) to the substantial increase in the number of publications; a lot more papers are being published, and due to the limited attention span of subsequent researchers, on average, papers are being forgotten faster. 

Past work on NLP papers and their citations includes work on gender bias (Schluter, 2018;Vogel and Jurafsky, 2012;Mohammad, 2020b), author location diversity (Rungta et al., 2022), author institution diversity (Abdalla et al., 2023), and on broad general trends such as average number of citations over time and by type of paper (Mohammad, 2020a,c;Wahle et al., 2022). Bollmann and Elliott (2020) were the first to explore the recency bias of citations in NLP papers. They showed that the ACL Anthology papers published between 2017 and 2019 cited more recent work than papers published between 2010 and 2014. Question 3 in Section 4 of our paper is of the same spirit that was explored in their work; however, our work examines a much larger spread of NLP papers (published between 1965 and 2021). This will shed light on the reproducibility of those findings and, more importantly, determine the broader trajectory of temporal citation patterns (from the start of ACL to present day). Additionally, our work introduces a new citation age diversity metric to quantify the degree of spread of citations over time, as well as an interactive online demo system to visualize the citation age diversity of any paper.

Title: How Deep Do Large Language Models Internalize Scientific Literature and Citation Practices?
Snippet: Figure 4 summarizes key characteristics, including publication year, number of authors, title length, and publication venue, for ground truth (blue, n=274, 951), generated (green, n=274, 497), existing generated (orange, n=116, 939), and non-existing generated (red, n=157, 558) references, indicating the model's internalization of citation patterns. The temporal distribution shows that generated references tend to be relatively more recent than ground truth references (Figure 4a), with the median difference being statistically significant as confirmed by a pairwise two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the focal paper level (p<0.001). The non-existent generated references amplify the recency bias documented in human citation behavior [93], while existing generated references show a more complex pattern: they under-cite earlier publications (pre-2000) compared to the ground truth, cite relatively more recent works between 2000 and 2012, and again under-cite in the most recent period, resulting in a median publication year equal to the ground truth. This temporal pattern of existing generated references suggests that their higher citation impact is not driven by a recency bias (Figure 3d, Appendix Figure A5b). The concentration of references in the 2000s reflects both ground truth and generated references peaking for papers published within 0-5 years before the focal paper (Appendix Figure A3c), as publications from this period would be recent relative to many focal papers in our 1999-2021 sample. 

The preference for smaller author teams emerges as another systematic pattern in generated references (Figure 4b). While ground truth references span author teams of 2-6 members, generated references concentrate on papers with 2-3 authors, and existing generated references focus even more narrowly on teams of 1-3 authors. This pattern, confirmed as statistically significant by a pairwise two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the focal paper level (p<0.001), stands in contrast to documented citation preferences for papers with larger author teams [29,96].

Title: How Deep Do Large Language Models Internalize Scientific Literature and Citation Practices?
Snippet: Current approaches to LLM-assisted scientific synthesis predominantly use document retrieval methods [28,56], complemented by model fine-tuning [57,89] or citation network navigation [85]. However, the reliance on search methods within external databases is unlikely to introduce significant new information dissemination patterns, potentially leading to effects similar to those observed with the introduction of comprehensive academic search tools [25,27,71]. We argue that as LLMs improve their capabilities of generating reference suggestions through the parametric knowledge acquired during training [4], scientists could leverage their internal world models [35,37] to make more informed decisions about which prior work to cite and build upon [100]. However, it remains unclear to what extent LLMs align with human citation practices, perform across domains, and may influence existing citation patterns. 

We address these questions on LLM-generated recommendations by comparing the characteristics of human citation patterns and reference suggestions generated by LLMs solely relying on their parametric knowledge. Scientific literature has long exhibited well-documented characteristics and potential biases in citation practices [10,59,87], which vary across fields [76,102,109], including preferences for recent publications [93], articles with shorter titles [55], papers from high-profile venues [53], and works with multiple authors [29,96], as well as the "Matthew effect," by which highly cited papers accumulate even more citations over time [52,74,104]. We argue that LLMs may introduce or exacerbate (field-specific) citation patterns [1,13,43,70,97] due to their struggle with long-tail knowledge [47] combined with uneven representation of scientific work in LLMs' training data [23,95]. While our experimental setup may not fully reflect real-world usage of LLMs for citation generation, which often involves more interactivity and reliance on external data sources, it provides a controlled laboratory setting to assess the parametric knowledge and inherent citation patterns of LLMs [12]. Understanding these patterns is crucial as they may influence how researchers discover and cite prior work, potentially reinforcing existing biases in scientific literature and shifting citation practices over time [33,80,83,92]. A1).

Title: Who Gets Cited? Gender- and Majority-Bias in LLM-Driven Reference Selection
Snippet: Beyond the studies on citaion accurarcy and performance (Byun, Vasicek, and Seppi 2024;Oami, Okada, and Nakada 2024;Mugaanyi et al. 2024;Nishikawa and Koshiba 2024), emerging evidence reveals that LLMs not only internalize but also systematically amplify human biases in scientific citation practices. Recent large-scale experiments (Algaba et al. 2025) demonstrate that when generating reference lists, LLMs strongly favor highly cited, more recent works, shorter paper titles, and prestigious publication venues-a phenomenon echoing and reinforcing the "Matthew effect" in science, where well-cited papers accrue disproportionate recognition. Other studies (Tian et al. 2024) confirm these trends and further find that LLM-generated recommendations mirror real-world team size and focus on incremental rather than highly disruptive research. However, ethnicity, gender, and country biases-well-documented in traditional citation patterns-are less pronounced or even slightly corrected in LLM outputs when compared to actual distributions. However, recent work (von Wedel et al. 2024) highlights that institutional prestige bias can persist or modestly increase in LLM-supported peer review. Overall, as LLMs integrate into research workflows, attention to their potential to exacerbate citation inequality remains critical (Zhang and Zhao 2025).

documents.snippet: Beyond the studies on citaion accurarcy and performance (Byun, Vasicek, and Seppi 2024;Oami, Okada, and Nakada 2024;Mugaanyi et al. 2024;Nishikawa and Koshiba 2024), emerging evidence reveals that LLMs not only internalize but also systematically amplify human biases in scientific citation practices. Recent large-scale experiments (Algaba et al. 2025) demonstrate that when generating reference lists, LLMs strongly favor highly cited, more recent works, shorter paper titles, and prestigious publication venues-a phenomenon echoing and reinforcing the "Matthew effect" in science, where well-cited papers accrue disproportionate recognition. Other studies (Tian et al. 2024) confirm these trends and further find that LLM-generated recommendations mirror real-world team size and focus on incremental rather than highly disruptive research. However, ethnicity, gender, and country biases-well-documented in traditional citation patterns-are less pronounced or even slightly corrected in LLM outputs when compared to actual distributions. However, recent work (von Wedel et al. 2024) highlights that institutional prestige bias can persist or modestly increase in LLM-supported peer review. Overall, as LLMs integrate into research workflows, attention to their potential to exacerbate citation inequality remains critical (Zhang and Zhao 2025).
