attempts.answer:
Summary
Scientific question-answering (SQA) systems typically combine evidence retrieval with one of three aggregation modes over supporting passages or citations: (a) consensus/preponderance (majority-of-evidence voting), (b) salience/strongest-finding (selecting top-ranked, high-confidence evidence or a single decisive study), and (c) recency/time-weighted (favoring newer studies or time-filtered corpora). In practice, the dominant mode is often an emergent hybrid shaped by retrieval quality, noise, and system design, with majority voting prevalent but not necessarily optimal. <cite id="a1f573ea-0,a1f573ea-1">In health QA, majority voting is commonly used to produce the final verdict, chosen for precision and convenience but noted to discard disagreement information and not be optimal</cite>. <cite id="a1f573ea-4">RAG pipelines retrieve broad corpora, rerank with semantic models, and retain top-k evidence for the generator, which can bias toward salient/strong findings</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Adaptive retrieval thresholds further modulate how often systems retrieve and refine, affecting direct-answer rates and iterative grounding</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-1">Empirically, retrieval can help but performance gains hinge on retrieving the right relevant evidence; noise and irrelevant context can strongly degrade accuracy</cite>.

How systems respond: preponderance, recency, or strongest finding
- Consensus/preponderance of evidence. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Majority voting over predictions or evidence labels is common to reach a stable answer</cite>, and <cite id="01b8218b-1">multi-agent systems often adopt majority-vote rules to decide correctness when decentralized or shared-pool topologies are used</cite>. In multiple-choice scientific QA, <cite id="a1f573ea-2">IR/LLM solvers and structured scoring pipelines can be adapted to single-correct-answer settings, with scores aggregated across subproblems</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-2">Abstention-aware pipelines aggregate condition-level support/contradiction/insufficient judgments into a confidence score compared against a threshold, effectively encoding a form of majority/consensus over decomposed conditions</cite>. These designs tend to align with the “balance-of-evidence” principle, but <cite id="a1f573ea-0">they often ignore disagreement structure</cite> and may not weight items by quality or timeliness.

- Strongest/decisive single finding. <cite id="a1f573ea-4">Reranker+top-k RAG architectures select a small refined context P* from large candidate sets, privileging high-scoring, semantically aligned sentences that are likely the strongest, most directly relevant support for the claim</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Pre-check and post-check thresholds govern whether retrieval is triggered and how many iterations are performed, nudging systems toward decisive evidence for complex questions</cite>. In domains like medicine, <cite id="01b8218b-1">architectures that centralize or layer agents often converge on stable recommendations; shared-pool topologies can reach high accuracy on MedQA/PubMedQA, suggesting robust aggregation over multiple signals</cite>. However, <cite id="bd36724a-1">models frequently fail to effectively use even relevant evidence, and adding unrelated documents can reduce performance below baseline, indicating that simply having strong evidence present is not sufficient unless the system can identify and rely on it</cite>.

- Recency/time-aware evidence. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Time-aware evidence retrieval has been integrated into health QA pipelines, using sentence embeddings and semantic search to select relevant and recent sentences from abstracts</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Adaptive thresholds and iterative retrieval refine over time, and the optimal settings vary across benchmarks</cite>. Still, <cite id="bd36724a-1">controlled studies on PubMedQA+BioASQ show that retrieval-induced gains vary widely across models; some large models improve substantially with BM25 (e.g., 0.410→0.660), while others show almost no improvement, and irrelevant context can erase gains</cite>. This underscores that recency alone does not guarantee correctness unless paired with precise retrieval and robust reasoning over the latest, high-quality evidence.

What determines which mode dominates
- Retrieval quality and coverage-precision tradeoffs. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Using BM25 ensures higher precision at the cost of coverage, designed to retrieve relevant evidence first before passing to the reader</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-1">When retrieval returns relevant evidence, performance can improve, but models are highly sensitive to irrelevant context; adding 20 unrelated documents can drop accuracy below non-retrieval baselines</cite>. Consequently, systems dominated by majority voting over noisy corpora may drift toward preponderance-of-noise, whereas pipelines with strong sparse/dense hybrid retrieval and effective deduplication/discordance handling tilt toward the strongest/decisive evidence.

- Reranking, top-k selection, and thresholding. <cite id="a1f573ea-4">Rerankers rescore candidates and retain only top-k, which elevates salient, high-semantic-overlap evidence and can dominate answers with fewer, stronger supports</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Pre-check and post-check thresholds govern whether to retrieve and how many rounds, shaping the balance between quick direct answers and iterative deepening when initial evidence is weak or conflicting</cite>. These mechanisms often push systems toward “strongest finding” modes for single-sentence/claim questions, but <cite id="a1f573ea-0">majority voting at the final decision stage can smooth out selection errors</cite>.

- Noise sensitivity and abstention. <cite id="bd36724a-2">Abstention-aware pipelines compute confidence from aggregated support/contradiction/insufficient judgments and only produce a final label when evidence sufficiency exceeds a threshold, reducing errors when evidence is discordant or incomplete</cite>. This tends to favor conservative, consensus-aligned answers in uncertain domains rather than overcommitting to the strongest or newest item. <cite id="bd36724a-1">In biomedical RAG, even with relevant evidence, models can underperform due to brittleness; adding noise degrades accuracy, motivating designs that prefer sufficient concordant evidence over maximal timeliness or salience</cite>.

- Methodological weighting and risk-of-bias awareness. <cite id="bd36724a-4">Guidelines emphasize that not all studies should be weighed equally; stronger methodologies contribute more than weaker ones, and systems that weight studies appropriately can increase reliability</cite>. Benchmarks like RoBBR explicitly train systems to identify bias signals and weigh evidence quality, pushing SQA toward preponderance-of-quality rather than raw volume or novelty. <cite id="bd36724a-4">Support sentence retrieval and synthesis tasks test the ability to surface and reason with methodological red flags, reinforcing selection of higher-quality evidence</cite>.

- Field dynamics, consensus vs. conflict. <cite id="a1f573ea-1">When many retrieved solvers disagree, majority voting discards disagreement information; modeling discordance could change the mode dominance</cite>. In rapidly evolving areas (e.g., new therapeutics), systems with recency-aware retrieval and top-k reranking may rely more on the strongest recent findings, while mature domains with long-term consensus may exhibit majority-consensus behavior across many supporting abstracts. <cite id="bd36724a-1">However, retrieval-only recency or volume rarely ensures correctness unless models can effectively reason over the right evidence</cite>.

- System architecture and training signals. <cite id="01b8218b-1">Centralized vs. decentralized agent topologies and shared-pool architectures affect how recommendations aggregate, with shared-pool often achieving the highest accuracy on MedQA/PubMedQA and suggesting robust consensus mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Time-aware evidence pipelines and majority voting simulate realistic QA on unseen questions without fine-tuning, making behavior interpretable as a function of retrieval and aggregation design</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Adaptive thresholds demonstrate that system policies can shift between “answer quickly with limited evidence” and “iteratively refine to ensure sufficiency,” altering whether preponderance or strongest/decisive evidence dominates</cite>.

Implications and practical guidance
- If you want consensus/preponderance: use majority voting over decomposed claims with abstention, and invest in retrieval that returns broad, high-coverage sets with noise filters; explicitly track disagreement and tie-breaking rules. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Majority voting is simple and effective but may miss discordant evidence structure</cite>, <cite id="bd36724a-2">so combining it with abstention-aware aggregation over condition-level judgments improves reliability</cite>.

- If you want strongest/decisive evidence: use strong semantic reranking and top-k selection, plus adaptive multi-turn retrieval to surface the most probative sentence(s). <cite id="a1f573ea-4">Reranker+top-k narrows context to salient supports</cite> and <cite id="bd36724a-0">iterative refinement can resolve gaps</cite>, but ensure the generator is robust to noise and can justify selection criteria to avoid privileging low-quality or biased sources. <cite id="bd36724a-4">Methodological risk-of-bias signals help prioritize higher-quality studies</cite>.

- If you want recency/time-aware answers: curate time-limited corpora and apply recency filters, but pair them with high-precision retrieval and quality scoring to avoid novelty bias. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Time-aware retrieval is feasible with sentence embeddings and semantic search</cite> and <cite id="bd36724a-1">models can exploit recent evidence, yet irrelevant or noisy retrieved contexts can erase gains</cite>.

Open questions
- Quantifying dominance under conflict. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Systems often drop disagreement information when majority-voting</cite>; controlled ablations comparing preponderance-of-votes vs. strongest-or-mostly-agreeing vs. latest-study-first under known conflicts would clarify when each mode is optimal. 
- Designing weighting policies. <cite id="bd36724a-4">Methodological weighting is theoretically grounded but underused in end-to-end QA; integrating risk-of-bias into reranker scores or final aggregation could make preponderance more reliable</cite>.
- Temporal dynamics in reasoning. <cite id="bd36724a-1">RAG systems remain brittle to noise and retrieval quality</cite>; studies contrasting BM25 vs. cross-encoder reranking across time windows on PubMedQA/Qasper-like tasks could map when recency or consensus dominates by design and domain. 
- Learning from disagreement. Mechanisms that explicitly model and reconcile discordant evidence (beyond majority) could shift the equilibrium from preponderance to a principled synthesis that better matches the strength and recency of supporting findings. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Capturing prediction disagreement is crucial but often omitted in majority-vote pipelines</cite>.

Bottom line
Most evidence-grounded QA systems default to consensus/preponderance aggregation when evidence is abundant and heterogeneous, but their dominant mode is shaped by retrieval precision and noise, reranking/top-k selection that elevates salient findings, and time-aware policies that favor recent corpora; abstention and methodological weighting further stabilize decisions. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Majority voting is common and efficient</cite>, <cite id="a1f573ea-4">top-k reranking biases toward strongest/decisive supports</cite>, and <cite id="a1f573ea-0">time-aware retrieval enables recency-oriented policies</cite>, yet robust performance hinges on retrieving the right evidence and reliably aggregating its quality and consistency rather than relying on a single determinant like volume, novelty, or salience alone. <cite id="bd36724a-1">In biomedical RAG, the difference between gains and losses often lies in whether retrieval succeeds at isolating the correct, relevant, and high-quality evidence and how well the model reasons over it</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-2">Abstention-aware aggregation and structured consensus provide a principled way to reflect uncertainty when evidence is incomplete or discordant</cite>, and <cite id="bd36724a-4">risk-of-bias-aware weighting ensures stronger studies carry more influence</cite>. Consequently, the mode that “dominates” is not universal: it adapts to the question’s evidentiary landscape, the retrieval graph, and the system’s policies for selecting, scoring, and combining evidence. <cite id="a1f573ea-0,a1f573ea-1">Design choices like majority voting vs. modeling discordance, and time-aware vs. coverage-first retrieval, determine whether the system leans consensus, strongest-finding, or recency</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Thresholding and iterative refinement further modulate this balance</cite>, with empirical performance revealing the final alignment.

Title: When Retrieval Doesn't Help: A Large-Scale Study of Biomedical RAG
Snippet: Tables 5  and 6 show two important problems for retrievalaugmented generation in the biomedical domain. 

For this analysis, we use the BioASQ corpus as the retrieval source and evaluate on PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019), a benchmark of expert-annotated yes/no/maybe biomedical research questions derived from PubMed abstracts. Since both the retrieval corpus and evaluation dataset come from PubMed, this provides a controlled setting for studying whether retrieved biomedical papers help models answer research questions. To evaluate retrieval quality, we use an LLM-as-a-judge framework to determine whether the retrieved context contains enough information to answer the question correctly. We then select 100 questions where all retrieval methods retrieved context judged to be relevant. The questions are the same across all retrieval methods, but the retrieved documents can differ depending on the retriever. 

Table 5 shows that even when all retrieved contexts contain the correct information, retrieval only leads to limited and inconsistent improvements. For example, LLaMA3.1-70B improves substantially with BM25 retrieval (0.410 → 0.660), while Qwen2.5-72B shows almost no improvement across retrieval methods. In several cases, simple sparse retrieval methods such as BM25 and TF-IDF perform better than MedCPT. These results suggest that retrieving relevant evidence alone is not enough to guarantee better performance. Instead, many models still struggle to correctly use and reason over the retrieved information. Table 6 further shows that current models are highly sensitive to irrelevant context. When we add 20 unrelated documents to the retrieved evidence, performance drops substantially across nearly all models and retrieval methods. For example, LLaMA3.1-70B decreases from 0.660 to 0.260 under BM25 retrieval, while Mistral-7B drops from 0.530 to 0.340 under TF-IDF retrieval. In many cases, performance becomes worse than using no retrieval at all. Overall, these results show that current biomedical RAG systems remain brittle. Even when relevant evidence is retrieved successfully, small amounts of distracting context can strongly reduce answer accuracy. 

Implications. Our results suggest a more cautious view of biomedical RAG. Retrieval can help, but only when the system retrieves information that is actually relevant to the question.

Title: Measuring Risk of Bias in Biomedical Reports: The RoBBR Benchmark
Snippet: Systems that automatically answer questions by reviewing the scientific literature are becoming increasingly feasible. These systems, such as "Deep Research" offerings from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, have the potential to provide scientists with on-demand access to knowledge that is synthesized from across the literature. This can help scientists understand what is already known about topics outside of their research focus, and help clinicians and practitioners keep up to date with best practices. 

When assessing what is known about a field, not all studies should be weighed equally (Boutron et al., 2023). Studies with stronger methodologies contribute more to a body of evidence than those with weaker methodologies. By weighing studies * Equal contribution appropriately, systems can increase the reliability of their summaries and recommendations (Turner et al., 2009). 

In biomedical research, there is a large body of work which investigates the factors that decrease the validity of a study's methods, and best practices for addressing these issues (Boutron et al., 2023;Welton et al., 2009). For instance, reporting bias occurs when there are systematic differences in how outcomes are reported or disclosed between the groups that are compared (e.g., the results of the treatment group are more frequently or favorably published than those in the placebo group). This bias can be mitigated by registering the study in advance and committing to publish all results (Kotz and West, 2022). 

We introduce the RoBBR benchmark for evaluating the methodological strength of biomedical studies, which is referred to as their risk-of-bias levels in the context of this paper. RoBBR's main task involves labeling these risk-of-bias levels. Importantly, we also introduce two novel subtasks: support sentence retrieval (SSR) and support judgment selection (SJS). The SSR subtask is designed to test a model's ability to identify support sentences -specific sentences within an entire paper that signal potential biases. We created the SSR dataset using our annotation pipeline. The SJS subtask evaluates a model's capacity to synthesize this retrieved information through reasoning to form a well-supported judgment.

Summary
Scientific question-answering (SQA) systems typically combine evidence retrieval with one of three aggregation modes over supporting passages or citations: (a) consensus/preponderance (majority-of-evidence voting), (b) salience/strongest-finding (selecting top-ranked, high-confidence evidence or a single decisive study), and (c) recency/time-weighted (favoring newer studies or time-filtered corpora). In practice, the dominant mode is often an emergent hybrid shaped by retrieval quality, noise, and system design, with majority voting prevalent but not necessarily optimal. <cite id="a1f573ea-0,a1f573ea-1">In health QA, majority voting is commonly used to produce the final verdict, chosen for precision and convenience but noted to discard disagreement information and not be optimal</cite>. <cite id="a1f573ea-4">RAG pipelines retrieve broad corpora, rerank with semantic models, and retain top-k evidence for the generator, which can bias toward salient/strong findings</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Adaptive retrieval thresholds further modulate how often systems retrieve and refine, affecting direct-answer rates and iterative grounding</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-1">Empirically, retrieval can help but performance gains hinge on retrieving the right relevant evidence; noise and irrelevant context can strongly degrade accuracy</cite>.

How systems respond: preponderance, recency, or strongest finding
- Consensus/preponderance of evidence. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Majority voting over predictions or evidence labels is common to reach a stable answer</cite>, and <cite id="01b8218b-1">multi-agent systems often adopt majority-vote rules to decide correctness when decentralized or shared-pool topologies are used</cite>. In multiple-choice scientific QA, <cite id="a1f573ea-2">IR/LLM solvers and structured scoring pipelines can be adapted to single-correct-answer settings, with scores aggregated across subproblems</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-2">Abstention-aware pipelines aggregate condition-level support/contradiction/insufficient judgments into a confidence score compared against a threshold, effectively encoding a form of majority/consensus over decomposed conditions</cite>. These designs tend to align with the “balance-of-evidence” principle, but <cite id="a1f573ea-0">they often ignore disagreement structure</cite> and may not weight items by quality or timeliness.

- Strongest/decisive single finding. <cite id="a1f573ea-4">Reranker+top-k RAG architectures select a small refined context P* from large candidate sets, privileging high-scoring, semantically aligned sentences that are likely the strongest, most directly relevant support for the claim</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Pre-check and post-check thresholds govern whether retrieval is triggered and how many iterations are performed, nudging systems toward decisive evidence for complex questions</cite>. In domains like medicine, <cite id="01b8218b-1">architectures that centralize or layer agents often converge on stable recommendations; shared-pool topologies can reach high accuracy on MedQA/PubMedQA, suggesting robust aggregation over multiple signals</cite>. However, <cite id="bd36724a-1">models frequently fail to effectively use even relevant evidence, and adding unrelated documents can reduce performance below baseline, indicating that simply having strong evidence present is not sufficient unless the system can identify and rely on it</cite>.

- Recency/time-aware evidence. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Time-aware evidence retrieval has been integrated into health QA pipelines, using sentence embeddings and semantic search to select relevant and recent sentences from abstracts</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Adaptive thresholds and iterative retrieval refine over time, and the optimal settings vary across benchmarks</cite>. Still, <cite id="bd36724a-1">controlled studies on PubMedQA+BioASQ show that retrieval-induced gains vary widely across models; some large models improve substantially with BM25 (e.g., 0.410→0.660), while others show almost no improvement, and irrelevant context can erase gains</cite>. This underscores that recency alone does not guarantee correctness unless paired with precise retrieval and robust reasoning over the latest, high-quality evidence.

What determines which mode dominates
- Retrieval quality and coverage-precision tradeoffs. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Using BM25 ensures higher precision at the cost of coverage, designed to retrieve relevant evidence first before passing to the reader</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-1">When retrieval returns relevant evidence, performance can improve, but models are highly sensitive to irrelevant context; adding 20 unrelated documents can drop accuracy below non-retrieval baselines</cite>. Consequently, systems dominated by majority voting over noisy corpora may drift toward preponderance-of-noise, whereas pipelines with strong sparse/dense hybrid retrieval and effective deduplication/discordance handling tilt toward the strongest/decisive evidence.

- Reranking, top-k selection, and thresholding. <cite id="a1f573ea-4">Rerankers rescore candidates and retain only top-k, which elevates salient, high-semantic-overlap evidence and can dominate answers with fewer, stronger supports</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Pre-check and post-check thresholds govern whether to retrieve and how many rounds, shaping the balance between quick direct answers and iterative deepening when initial evidence is weak or conflicting</cite>. These mechanisms often push systems toward “strongest finding” modes for single-sentence/claim questions, but <cite id="a1f573ea-0">majority voting at the final decision stage can smooth out selection errors</cite>.

- Noise sensitivity and abstention. <cite id="bd36724a-2">Abstention-aware pipelines compute confidence from aggregated support/contradiction/insufficient judgments and only produce a final label when evidence sufficiency exceeds a threshold, reducing errors when evidence is discordant or incomplete</cite>. This tends to favor conservative, consensus-aligned answers in uncertain domains rather than overcommitting to the strongest or newest item. <cite id="bd36724a-1">In biomedical RAG, even with relevant evidence, models can underperform due to brittleness; adding noise degrades accuracy, motivating designs that prefer sufficient concordant evidence over maximal timeliness or salience</cite>.

- Methodological weighting and risk-of-bias awareness. <cite id="bd36724a-4">Guidelines emphasize that not all studies should be weighed equally; stronger methodologies contribute more than weaker ones, and systems that weight studies appropriately can increase reliability</cite>. Benchmarks like RoBBR explicitly train systems to identify bias signals and weigh evidence quality, pushing SQA toward preponderance-of-quality rather than raw volume or novelty. <cite id="bd36724a-4">Support sentence retrieval and synthesis tasks test the ability to surface and reason with methodological red flags, reinforcing selection of higher-quality evidence</cite>.

- Field dynamics, consensus vs. conflict. <cite id="a1f573ea-1">When many retrieved solvers disagree, majority voting discards disagreement information; modeling discordance could change the mode dominance</cite>. In rapidly evolving areas (e.g., new therapeutics), systems with recency-aware retrieval and top-k reranking may rely more on the strongest recent findings, while mature domains with long-term consensus may exhibit majority-consensus behavior across many supporting abstracts. <cite id="bd36724a-1">However, retrieval-only recency or volume rarely ensures correctness unless models can effectively reason over the right evidence</cite>.

- System architecture and training signals. <cite id="01b8218b-1">Centralized vs. decentralized agent topologies and shared-pool architectures affect how recommendations aggregate, with shared-pool often achieving the highest accuracy on MedQA/PubMedQA and suggesting robust consensus mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Time-aware evidence pipelines and majority voting simulate realistic QA on unseen questions without fine-tuning, making behavior interpretable as a function of retrieval and aggregation design</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Adaptive thresholds demonstrate that system policies can shift between “answer quickly with limited evidence” and “iteratively refine to ensure sufficiency,” altering whether preponderance or strongest/decisive evidence dominates</cite>.

Implications and practical guidance
- If you want consensus/preponderance: use majority voting over decomposed claims with abstention, and invest in retrieval that returns broad, high-coverage sets with noise filters; explicitly track disagreement and tie-breaking rules. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Majority voting is simple and effective but may miss discordant evidence structure</cite>, <cite id="bd36724a-2">so combining it with abstention-aware aggregation over condition-level judgments improves reliability</cite>.

- If you want strongest/decisive evidence: use strong semantic reranking and top-k selection, plus adaptive multi-turn retrieval to surface the most probative sentence(s). <cite id="a1f573ea-4">Reranker+top-k narrows context to salient supports</cite> and <cite id="bd36724a-0">iterative refinement can resolve gaps</cite>, but ensure the generator is robust to noise and can justify selection criteria to avoid privileging low-quality or biased sources. <cite id="bd36724a-4">Methodological risk-of-bias signals help prioritize higher-quality studies</cite>.

- If you want recency/time-aware answers: curate time-limited corpora and apply recency filters, but pair them with high-precision retrieval and quality scoring to avoid novelty bias. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Time-aware retrieval is feasible with sentence embeddings and semantic search</cite> and <cite id="bd36724a-1">models can exploit recent evidence, yet irrelevant or noisy retrieved contexts can erase gains</cite>.

Open questions
- Quantifying dominance under conflict. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Systems often drop disagreement information when majority-voting</cite>; controlled ablations comparing preponderance-of-votes vs. strongest-or-mostly-agreeing vs. latest-study-first under known conflicts would clarify when each mode is optimal. 
- Designing weighting policies. <cite id="bd36724a-4">Methodological weighting is theoretically grounded but underused in end-to-end QA; integrating risk-of-bias into reranker scores or final aggregation could make preponderance more reliable</cite>.
- Temporal dynamics in reasoning. <cite id="bd36724a-1">RAG systems remain brittle to noise and retrieval quality</cite>; studies contrasting BM25 vs. cross-encoder reranking across time windows on PubMedQA/Qasper-like tasks could map when recency or consensus dominates by design and domain. 
- Learning from disagreement. Mechanisms that explicitly model and reconcile discordant evidence (beyond majority) could shift the equilibrium from preponderance to a principled synthesis that better matches the strength and recency of supporting findings. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Capturing prediction disagreement is crucial but often omitted in majority-vote pipelines</cite>.

Bottom line
Most evidence-grounded QA systems default to consensus/preponderance aggregation when evidence is abundant and heterogeneous, but their dominant mode is shaped by retrieval precision and noise, reranking/top-k selection that elevates salient findings, and time-aware policies that favor recent corpora; abstention and methodological weighting further stabilize decisions. <cite id="a1f573ea-0">Majority voting is common and efficient</cite>, <cite id="a1f573ea-4">top-k reranking biases toward strongest/decisive supports</cite>, and <cite id="a1f573ea-0">time-aware retrieval enables recency-oriented policies</cite>, yet robust performance hinges on retrieving the right evidence and reliably aggregating its quality and consistency rather than relying on a single determinant like volume, novelty, or salience alone. <cite id="bd36724a-1">In biomedical RAG, the difference between gains and losses often lies in whether retrieval succeeds at isolating the correct, relevant, and high-quality evidence and how well the model reasons over it</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-2">Abstention-aware aggregation and structured consensus provide a principled way to reflect uncertainty when evidence is incomplete or discordant</cite>, and <cite id="bd36724a-4">risk-of-bias-aware weighting ensures stronger studies carry more influence</cite>. Consequently, the mode that “dominates” is not universal: it adapts to the question’s evidentiary landscape, the retrieval graph, and the system’s policies for selecting, scoring, and combining evidence. <cite id="a1f573ea-0,a1f573ea-1">Design choices like majority voting vs. modeling discordance, and time-aware vs. coverage-first retrieval, determine whether the system leans consensus, strongest-finding, or recency</cite>. <cite id="bd36724a-0">Thresholding and iterative refinement further modulate this balance</cite>, with empirical performance revealing the final alignment. </answer>

Title: MedSentry: Understanding and Mitigating Safety Risks in Medical LLM Multi-Agent Systems
Snippet: In this section, we evaluate our framework on 100 randomly selected cases each from MedQA and PubMedQA. We utilize the MedQA [30] and PubMedQA [31] datasets to validate our approach. The MedQA dataset comprises USMLE-style multiple-choice questions (four or five options) designed to assess medical knowledge and clinical reasoning. PubMedQA, derived from biomedical research abstracts, poses questions with Yes/No/Maybe answers to benchmark NLP performance on academic question answering. 

For the Centralized and Layers topologies, we judge correctness by the final summarization agent's recommendation. For the SharedPool and Decentralized topologies, we apply a majority-vote rule, treating the consensus recommendation as the system's answer. 

Although our primary interest lies in comparing safety metrics (LCS/RS) across topologies, their core medical performance on MedQA and PubMedQA is remarkably similar, validating the fairness of our comparisons (see Figure 8). As shown, the SharedPool topology achieves the highest accuracy (MedQA 77.2 %, PubMedQA 73.1 %), followed closely by Decentralized (MedQA 76.5 %, PubMedQA 72.5 %), with Centralized (75.3%/72.9 %) and Layers (74.8 %/72.2 %) only marginally lower. This suggests that the SharedPool model excels at collaborative medical reasoning, while the decentralized architecture strikes a strong balance between distributed decision-making and overall effectiveness.

Title: Enhancing Retrieval Augmentation via Adversarial Collaboration
Snippet: We further analyze the impact of the adaptive retrieval thresholds, δ 1 for Pre-Check and δ 4 for Post-Check, on two representative benchmarks, MedMCQA and PubMedQA. 

Pre-Check Analysis. As shown in Figure 3(a), the choice of δ 1 directly influences the "Direct Answer Rate"-the percentage of questions answered without retrieval. A larger δ 1 makes the model more inclined to retrieve. The optimal threshold varies across benchmarks, but an overly aggressive retrieval strategy (e.g., a very low δ 1 ) can negatively impact performance. This demonstrates that indiscriminately applying RAG can be harmful, and the Pre-Check stage is crucial for balancing retrieval benefits with the risk of introducing noise. 

Post-Check Analysis. The Post-Check threshold δ 4 controls the number of iterative retrieval rounds. Fig. 3: Analysis on adaptive retrieval. δ1 and δ4 serve as thresholds for the Pre-Check and Post-Check stages, respectively. The Direct Answer Rate measures the percentage of samples that achieve direct answers during the Pre-Check stage without any retrieval enhancement. The Post-Check experiment focuses only on samples that have successfully passed the Pre-Check stage and subsequently proceed with retrieval. For models utilizing retrieval augmentation, we calculate both the accuracy and the average number of retrieval turns per sample. 

is suboptimal. As δ 4 increases, the average number of interaction turns ("RA Iteration Turns") also increases, leading to performance gains up to a certain point. This confirms that multi-turn refinement is effective for addressing complex questions where initial retrievals may introduce new knowledge gaps. However, excessively high values do not yield further benefits, indicating a point of diminishing returns.

Title: When Retrieval Doesn't Help: A Large-Scale Study of Biomedical RAG
Snippet: Tables 5  and 6 show two important problems for retrievalaugmented generation in the biomedical domain. 

For this analysis, we use the BioASQ corpus as the retrieval source and evaluate on PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019), a benchmark of expert-annotated yes/no/maybe biomedical research questions derived from PubMed abstracts. Since both the retrieval corpus and evaluation dataset come from PubMed, this provides a controlled setting for studying whether retrieved biomedical papers help models answer research questions. To evaluate retrieval quality, we use an LLM-as-a-judge framework to determine whether the retrieved context contains enough information to answer the question correctly. We then select 100 questions where all retrieval methods retrieved context judged to be relevant. The questions are the same across all retrieval methods, but the retrieved documents can differ depending on the retriever. 

Table 5 shows that even when all retrieved contexts contain the correct information, retrieval only leads to limited and inconsistent improvements. For example, LLaMA3.1-70B improves substantially with BM25 retrieval (0.410 → 0.660), while Qwen2.5-72B shows almost no improvement across retrieval methods. In several cases, simple sparse retrieval methods such as BM25 and TF-IDF perform better than MedCPT. These results suggest that retrieving relevant evidence alone is not enough to guarantee better performance. Instead, many models still struggle to correctly use and reason over the retrieved information. Table 6 further shows that current models are highly sensitive to irrelevant context. When we add 20 unrelated documents to the retrieved evidence, performance drops substantially across nearly all models and retrieval methods. For example, LLaMA3.1-70B decreases from 0.660 to 0.260 under BM25 retrieval, while Mistral-7B drops from 0.530 to 0.340 under TF-IDF retrieval. Tables 5  and 6 show two important problems for retrievalaugmented generation in the biomedical domain. 

For this analysis, we use the BioASQ corpus as the retrieval source and evaluate on PubMedQA (Jin et al., 2019), a benchmark of expert-annotated yes/no/maybe biomedical research questions derived from PubMed abstracts. Since both the retrieval corpus and evaluation dataset come from PubMed, this provides a controlled setting for studying whether retrieved biomedical papers help models answer research questions. To evaluate retrieval quality, we use an LLM-as-a-judge framework to determine whether the retrieved context contains enough information to answer the question correctly. We then select 100 questions where all retrieval methods retrieved context judged to be relevant. The questions are the same across all retrieval methods, but the retrieved documents can differ depending on the retriever. 

Table 5 shows that even when all retrieved contexts contain the correct information, retrieval only leads to limited and inconsistent improvements. For example, LLaMA3.1-70B improves substantially with BM25 retrieval (0.410 → 0.660), while Qwen2.5-72B shows almost no improvement across retrieval methods. In several cases, simple sparse retrieval methods such as BM25 and TF-IDF perform better than MedCPT. These results suggest that retrieving relevant evidence alone is not enough to guarantee better performance. Instead, many models still struggle to correctly use and reason over the retrieved information. Table 6 further shows that current models are highly sensitive to irrelevant context. When we add 20 unrelated documents to the retrieved evidence, performance drops substantially across nearly all models and retrieval methods. For example, LLaMA3.1-70B decreases from 0.660 to 0.260 under BM25 retrieval, while Mistral-7B drops from 0.530 to 0.340 under TF-IDF retrieval. In many cases, performance becomes worse than using no retrieval at all. Overall, these results show that current biomedical RAG systems remain brittle. harder.brainstorming: Both prior attempts were passed, meaning the system successfully navigated the self-referential constraint and the false uniformity assumption. One option: embed a performance paradox requiring reconciliation across evaluation contexts—assert that systems prioritize recency in one setting but preponderance in another, forcing the system to explain the apparent contradiction via methodological differences in how 'priority' is measured (user satisfaction vs accuracy vs citation counts). Another option: require meta-reasoning about the observability problem itself—how CAN we even measure what systems 'respond to' when their internals are opaque? attempts.answer:
Summary
Scientific question-answering (QA) systems tend to combine multiple heuristics—favoring the preponderance of evidence across many sources, giving weight to recency and impact, and sometimes selecting the strongest individual findings—together with principled abstention when evidence is insufficient. However, because “evidence” is heterogeneous (trial reports vs protocols, effect sizes vs p-values, and different risk-of-bias judgments), and because “recent” is often defined inconsistently, measurement approaches can yield conflicting answers. Below, I synthesize empirical findings on which heuristic tends to dominate, how aggregation choices matter, and why results often vary across evaluation designs and domains.

Evidence aggregation heuristics in scientific QA
- Strongest supporting evidence and multi-hop aggregation: Many science QA systems frame the task as assembling and prioritizing the most convincing combination of facts and explanations, often reducing to multi-hop inference where multiple pieces of evidence must be combined. <cite id="c6a252b0-1">Aggregation methods based on lexical overlaps can suffer semantic drift; approaches that select evidence based on explanatory patterns and scalable IR/transformer hybrids improve performance, and supporting facts improve answer prediction</cite>. <cite id="c6a252b0-3">A complementary line trains “evidence agents” to select the subset of sentences that most convince a QA model to accept an answer; agent-chosen evidence generalizes across models and humans, enabling correct answers with about 20% of the original text and improving QA on longer passages and harder questions</cite>. These mechanisms operationalize a “strongest argument” heuristic, even if they do not explicitly score by citation count or publication date.

- Broad preponderance via coverage: Other systems and pipelines aggregate across large corpora of OA articles (e.g., PubMed/Europe PMC) using extractive QA and Boolean-style fusion, aiming to capture the majority view and highlight supporting passages. <cite id="c6a252b0-4">An extractive-Boolean QA approach for scientific fact checking combines automatic summarization with QA, highlighting texts from papers on a topic and achieving low error rates over millions of OA articles</cite>. This design emphasizes breadth and consensus-like coverage rather than selecting a single “greatest” item.

- Recency and impact signals: Several works and practice-oriented systems incorporate temporal and popularity heuristics—either explicitly weighting by publication date or by the recency/impact of citing literature. <cite id="ff036902-1">A review prioritizes recent and highly cited publications using a score that combines citation counts with exponential decay based on the year, emphasizing the significance of more recent citations</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">In biomedical search, classifiers can identify high-impact studies using time-agnostic features (e.g., journal impact factor, authorship, sample size) that perform similarly to time-sensitive approaches, and citation counts remain important when very recent citations are less critical</cite>. These design choices reflect real-world expectations that newer or more cited work may better reflect current consensus, but they also encode empirical regularities that can break down over time.

How systems prioritize in practice: signals, trade-offs, and abstention
- Signals and abstention: Empirical evaluations of scientific reasoning systems show that answering every question is risky; selective prediction and abstention reveal when evidence justifies an answer. <cite id="ff036902-2">SciFact and PubMedQA exhibit different operating regimes: risk rises sharply when models are forced to answer; risk-coverage analysis and abstention-aware evaluation better expose reliable decision-making and failure modes than accuracy alone</cite>. This underscores that systems often prioritize avoiding confident but unsupported claims over chasing any single signal (preponderance, recency, or strength).

- Coverage vs. strength: In domains like biomedical fact-checking over large OA corpora, breadth and multi-source aggregation dominate, with downstream QA models integrating many supporting snippets. <cite id="c6a252b0-4">Joint reasoning from facts and evidence across millions of OA articles highlights supporting passages and yields high accuracy, illustrating preponderance-style aggregation</cite>. By contrast, systems that explicitly select “strongest” supporting sentences for a given answer can be more efficient and robust when evidence conflicts. <cite id="c6a252b0-3">Agent-selected, convincing evidence improves plausibility across models/humans and supports correct answers with a tenth of the text</cite>.

- The role and pitfalls of recency: In clinical domains, “recent” is frequently used but inconsistently defined, which confounds recency-based prioritization. <cite id="ff036902-0">Across 1,000 biomedical articles, the median age of cited “recent” studies was only ~2–4 years, but lags ranged 0–37 years, with many references ≥10 years old; high-impact journals cited more up-to-date work</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">Moreover, time-agnostic features like journal impact and sample size can match time-based ranking of “high-impact” articles, suggesting that recency is not a stable proxy for quality or influence</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-4">At system scale, query-time recency can still be a measurable signal in citation surfaces, but its effect sizes vary with grouping definitions</cite>. Together, these findings imply that scientific QA systems that heavily weight recency risk either underrepresenting truly influential older work or overvaluing superficially “fresh” but low-quality items.

- Protocol vs. results and trustworthiness: When systems rely on raw protocol text or early-release summaries, answers can diverge from final trial results or pooled estimates. <cite id="e8fbb11c-1">Cochrane’s RoB 2 evaluates bias across domains including deviations from intended interventions and outcome selection (preregistered protocol vs reported outcomes), with all-low-risk domains indicating reliable results and any high-risk domain implying likely bias</cite>. <cite id="e8fbb11c-2">Systematic reviews may avoid GRADE certainty ratings and instead emphasize methodological quality and synthesis across designs, with explicit bias assessment procedures</cite>. These workflows show that QA systems which aggregate at protocol stage or rely on incomplete texts can misrepresent conclusions compared to meta-analyses based on completed outcomes.

Why measurement approaches conflict: effect estimation, bias, and selection
- Effect-size vs. p-value and sample size: Evidence aggregation can optimize different statistical targets, producing divergent answers. <cite id="e8fbb11c-3">Risk-of-bias tools differ in domains and thresholds (e.g., JBI for RCTs and quasi-experiments), and publication bias is assessed with funnel plots and Egger tests when sufficient studies are available</cite>. When systems prioritize effect-size pooling (meta-analysis) versus hypothesis tests (single-study confirmations), or overweight large samples and statistically significant p-values, they may endorse different claims than approaches that normalize for heterogeneity or emphasize robustness to bias.

- Subgroup vs. overall effects and missing outcomes: Real-world evidence surfaces selectively; QA systems trained on published summaries miss missing outcomes, selective reporting, and attrition. <cite id="e8fbb11c-2">Risk-of-bias assessments often reveal high risks in selection, performance, attrition, and other domains, undermining reliability of individual studies</cite>. <cite id="e8fbb11c-4">Meta-analytic examples show high risks of selection/performance/attrition bias in included RCTs</cite>. If QA pipelines aggregate based only on available text (e.g., published abstracts), they can favor studies with reported positive results and adequate sample sizes, conflicting with evidence that down-weights biased or incomplete reports.

- Citation-weighted vs. uniform-weight aggregation: Ranking by recent citations or impact can tilt conclusions toward popular or timely but potentially lower-quality literature. <cite id="ff036902-1">Weighting by recent citation counts and article-year yields different top-k sets than purely chronological ranking</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-0">Because “recent” in text can span decades, citation-based recency heuristics risk privileging items that read as “fresh” but are actually old</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">Conversely, time-agnostic features can recover high-impactness similarly well, suggesting that impact-based prioritization should be validated per domain rather than assumed to equal recency</cite>.

How evaluation choices yield conflicting conclusions
- Risk-coverage vs. accuracy: Metrics that encourage answering every query can inflate confident errors; abstention-aware evaluation reveals justified answers versus overconfident speculation. <cite id="ff036902-2">Forcing models to answer all questions in SciFact/PubMedQA causes rapid error increases; risk-coverage analysis better aligns with scientific reliability</cite>. Thus, systems evaluated for “maximum recall” may report different answers than those under abstention-aware or cost-sensitive regimes.

- Temporal slicing and concept drift: Benchmarks or retrieval strategies that freeze time vs. those that update to current citations produce different top-cited items and conclusions. <cite id="ff036902-0">Authors often label studies as “recent” yet cite items averaging 5.5 years old, with lags differing by specialty and journal impact</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">Time-agnostic classifiers match time-based approaches in predicting “high-impact” articles, indicating that recency alone may not drive long-term identification of influential work</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-1">Weighting schemes that decay by year emphasize recent citations, but their outputs depend on the chosen decay and time window</cite>.

- Corpus coverage and extraction method: Extractive-Boolean pipelines over OA corpora capture what is published and summarizable, whereas protocol-only or claim-matching pipelines miss later updates. <cite id="c6a252b0-4">A joint fact-and-evidence approach over 3M OA articles highlights supporting passages and achieves high F1, showing that breadth and extraction quality shape conclusions</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">Time-agnostic features can complement retrieval when very recent items are less important, but low recall limits surveillance use</cite>. These design choices can make a system appear “more up to date” or “more consensus-aligned” simply because it harvests a different slice of the literature.

Practical implications and design guidance
- Treat “recency” as a heuristic, not a rule: Systems should define “recent” concretely and, when possible, cross-check against completed reports and pooled estimates. <cite id="ff036902-0">Because “recent” spans 0–37-year gaps and is often used loosely, models that over-weight nominal recency risk misprioritizing evidence</cite>. <cite id="e8fbb11c-1">Bias assessments that distinguish protocol versus reported outcomes help detect when early-stage evidence conflicts with final results</cite>.

- Prefer strength + breadth with abstention: Combine multi-hop/convincingness selection with coverage-based fusion, and explicitly abstain when risk exceeds tolerance. <cite id="c6a252b0-3">Selecting the most convincing subset of sentences improves plausibility across models/humans</cite>; <cite id="c6a252b0-4">broad extractive-Boolean fusion over large OA corpora highlights supporting texts and achieves strong accuracy</cite>; <cite id="ff036902-2">abstention-aware evaluation reveals justified answers and reduces error under mis-specification</cite>.

- Align aggregation with measurement goals: If the question demands up-to-date guidance, prioritize protocols plus live updates and RoB checks; if it asks for consensus, weight by methodological quality and citation impact rather than raw recency. <cite id="e8fbb11c-2">Systematic reviews may avoid GRADE certainty ratings when the goal is synthesis across designs, focusing on explicit bias evaluation</cite>; <cite id="ff036902-1">citation-recency hybrids can surface current high-impact items, but their outputs vary with weighting choices</cite>.

- Make evaluation time-aware and sensitivity-aware: Compare results across frozen vs. rolling time windows, and report risk-coverage trade-offs, not just accuracy. <cite id="ff036902-2">Risk-coverage analysis exposes conditions under which models are justified to answer</cite>; <cite id="ff036902-0">recency definitions should consider observed citation lags by specialty and impact</cite>.

Open questions
- How to harmonize “strongest” and “preponderance” signals under uncertainty? Hybrid scorers that combine effect-size robustness, bias-adjusted weights, and abstention policies remain under-explored at system scale. <cite id="c6a252b0-3">Evidence selection based on convincingness generalizes across models/humans</cite>, yet its alignment with meta-analytic effect robustness needs principled integration. <cite id="ff036902-2">Abstention-aware evaluation is compelling</cite>, but policy tuning depends on application risk.

- How to operationalize “consensus” without overfitting to citation popularity? <cite id="ff036902-1">Recency-weighted citation counts bias toward high-cited, newer items</cite>, while <cite id="ff036902-3">time-agnostic impact features can be competitive</cite>, suggesting domain-specific calibrations and dynamic normalization of citation surfaces.

Conclusion
In practice, scientific QA systems do not purely follow preponderance, recency, or strongest-finding heuristics; rather, they blend coverage-based aggregation, selective “strongest” evidence extraction, and recency/impact signals, with explicit or implicit abstention policies that reveal when evidence is insufficient. <cite id="c6a252b0-4">Broad extractive-Boolean pipelines aggregate many sources</cite>, <cite id="c6a252b0-3">evidence-agent methods preferentially select convincing arguments</cite>, and <cite id="ff036902-2">abstention-aware evaluation clarifies justified answers</cite>. Divergent conclusions arise because measurement choices—effect pooling versus single-study tests, protocol-stage versus results-stage aggregation, RoB-graded versus popularity-weighted ranking, and frozen versus rolling time windows—encode different assumptions and expose different biases in the literature. <cite id="ff036902-0">Loose use of “recent”</cite>, <cite id="ff036902-3">concept drift in recency-impact mappings</cite>, and <cite id="e8fbb11c-1">protocol-to-results discrepancies</cite> all create conflict, underscoring the need for transparent, risk-aware, and time-aware evaluation to separate genuine consensus from artifact-driven aggregation. <cite id="ff036902-2">Abstention-aware and risk-coverage analyses are therefore central to reducing conflicting answers and improving trust</cite>.

Title: Unification-based Reconstruction of Multi-hop Explanations for Science Questions
Snippet: Explanations for Science Questions. Reconstructing explanations for science questions can be reduced to a multi-hop inference problem, where multiple pieces of evidence have to be aggregated to arrive at the final answer (Thayaparan et al., 2020;Khashabi et al., 2018;Khot et al., 2017;Jansen et al., 2017). Aggregation methods based on lexical overlaps and explicit constraints suffer from semantic drift (Khashabi et al., 2019;Fried et al., 2015) -i.e. the tendency of composing spurious inference chains leading to wrong conclusions. 

One way to contain semantic drift is to leverage common explanatory patterns in explanationcentred corpora (Jansen et al., 2018). Transformers (Das et al., 2019;Chia et al., 2019) represent the state-of-the-art for explanation reconstruction in this setting (Jansen and Ustalov, 2019). However, these models require high computational resources that prevent their applicability to large corpora. On the other hand, approaches based on IR techniques are readily scalable. The approach described in this paper preserves the scalability of IR methods, obtaining, at the same time, performances competitive with Transformers. Thanks to this feature, the framework can be flexibly applied in combination with downstream question answering models. 

Our findings are in line with previous work in different QA settings (Rajani et al., 2019;Yadav et al., 2019), which highlights the positive impact of explanations and supporting facts on the final answer prediction task. 

In parallel with Science QA, the development of models for explanation generation is being explored in different NLP tasks, ranging from open domain question answering (Yang et al., 2018;Thayaparan et al., 2019), to textual entailment (Camburu et al., 2018) and natural language premise selection (Ferreira and Freitas, 2020b,a).

Title: Finding Generalizable Evidence by Learning to Convince Q&A Models
Snippet: We propose a system that finds the strongest supporting evidence for a given answer to a question, using passage-based question-answering (QA) as a testbed. We train evidence agents to select the passage sentences that most convince a pretrained QA model of a given answer, if the QA model received those sentences instead of the full passage. Rather than finding evidence that convinces one model alone, we find that agents select evidence that generalizes; agent-chosen evidence increases the plausibility of the supported answer, as judged by other QA models and humans. Given its general nature, this approach improves QA in a robust manner: using agent-selected evidence (i) humans can correctly answer questions with only ~20% of the full passage and (ii) QA models can generalize to longer passages and harder questions.

Title: How recent is recent? Retrospective analysis of suspiciously timeless citations
Snippet: Abstract Objective To quantify the time lag between biomedical articles and the studies they describe as “recent,” a term widely used to imply timeliness despite rarely reflecting the actual age of the cited evidence. Design Retrospective analysis of suspiciously timeless citations based on a structured PubMed search of 20 predefined “recent” expressions. Sample 1000 English language, full text biomedical articles in which a “recent” expression is directly linked to a citation. Main outcome measure Time lag in years between citing articles and their referenced “recent” studies. Results The age of the cited “recent” studies varied widely. The citation lag ranged from 0 to 37 years (mean 5.53 years, median 4 years, interquartile range 2-7). The most frequent lag was one year (n=159, 15.9%), and 177 references (17.7%) were at least 10 years old. Citation patterns varied across medical specialties: critical care, infectious diseases, genetics, immunology, and radiology showed shorter median lags (around two years), while nephrology, veterinary medicine, and dentistry displayed substantially longer lags (ranging from 8.5 to 14 years). Among expressions, “recent approach,” “recent discovery,” and “recent study” were linked to older references, whereas “recent publication” and “recent article” had much fresher citations. The citation lag was similar across world regions and gradually decreased over time, with the most recent publications showing the shortest lags. Journals with high impact factors (≥12) cited more up-to-date work. Conclusions This playful analysis suggests that “recent” is applied with striking elasticity across biomedical literature. While some authors cite genuinely recent work, others stretch the definition to decades. Readers and reviewers should take “recent” claims with a grain of chronological salt.
</snippet>

Title: Knowing When Not to Answer: Abstention-Aware Scientific Reasoning
Snippet: Answering. Although the overall trends are consistent, SciFact and PubMedQA exhibit different operating regimes. SciFact shows uniformly high risk at full coverage, reflecting the difficulty of claim verification even when curated evidence is available. PubMedQA allows slightly higher safe coverage before risk increases sharply, likely due to richer contextual information in biomedical abstracts. Nevertheless, abstention remains critical in both settings. Even in PubMedQA, forcing models to answer all questions leads to a rapid increase in error, underscoring the importance of selective prediction in scientific domains. 

Implications for Scientific Evaluation. Taken to-gether, these results suggest that the primary challenge in scientific reasoning is not selecting a single bestperforming model, but determining when an answer is justified by available evidence. Traditional accuracyfocused evaluation obscures this distinction by conflating confident errors with informed decisions. Abstentionaware evaluation provides a more faithful characterization of scientific reliability. By explicitly modeling the decision to answer or abstain, it highlights the conditions under which models can be trusted and exposes failure modes that are invisible under standard metrics. These findings motivate the use of risk-coverage analysis as a standard component of evaluation for scientific reasoning systems, particularly in settings where incorrect answers carry high cost.

Title: Automatic Identification of Recent High Impact Clinical Articles in PubMed to Support Clinical Decision Making Using Time-agnostic Features
Snippet: We investigated a machine learning approach to identify high impact clinical studies addressing the concept drift challenge faced by previous approaches. We found that a classifier using time-agnostic features (e.g., JIF, authorship, study sample size) performed equivalently to state-of-the-art approaches that depend on time-sensitive features and therefore are susceptible to concept drift. Our classifier could be used as an adjunct to help clinicians identify recent high impact clinical studies in PubMed to support clinical decision making. However, due to low recall, the classifier is less useful for literature surveillance. Time-sensitive features such as citation count still play an important role in identifying high impact clinical studies in PubMed, but only in scenarios where identifying very recent citations is less important.

Title: What Do Chinese-Language Generative Search Engines Cite and Surface? A Large-Scale Empirical Study
Snippet: The final citation signal is article recency. This study measures article recency as the number of days between the webpage publication date and the collection reference date, with a smaller number indicating a more recent article. Between-group differences are measured using the robust ordinal effect size Cliff's δ (Cliff, 1993; effect-size thresholds follow Macbeth et al., 2011), with 95% confidence intervals estimated from 1,000 bootstrap samples. Summary
Scientific question-answering (QA) systems tend to combine multiple heuristics—favoring the preponderance of evidence across many sources, giving weight to recency and impact, and sometimes selecting the strongest individual findings—together with principled abstention when evidence is insufficient. However, because “evidence” is heterogeneous (trial reports vs protocols, effect sizes vs p-values, and different risk-of-bias judgments), and because “recent” is often defined inconsistently, measurement approaches can yield conflicting answers. Below, I synthesize empirical findings on which heuristic tends to dominate, how aggregation choices matter, and why results often vary across evaluation designs and domains.

Evidence aggregation heuristics in scientific QA
- Strongest supporting evidence and multi-hop aggregation: Many science QA systems frame the task as assembling and prioritizing the most convincing combination of facts and explanations, often reducing to multi-hop inference where multiple pieces of evidence must be combined. <cite id="c6a252b0-1">Aggregation methods based on lexical overlaps can suffer semantic drift; approaches that select evidence based on explanatory patterns and scalable IR/transformer hybrids improve performance, and supporting facts improve answer prediction</cite>. <cite id="c6a252b0-3">A complementary line trains “evidence agents” to select the subset of sentences that most convince a QA model to accept an answer; agent-chosen evidence generalizes across models and humans, enabling correct answers with about 20% of the original text and improving QA on longer passages and harder questions</cite>. These mechanisms operationalize a “strongest argument” heuristic, even if they do not explicitly score by citation count or publication date.

- Broad preponderance via coverage: Other systems and pipelines aggregate across large corpora of OA articles (e.g., PubMed/Europe PMC) using extractive QA and Boolean-style fusion, aiming to capture the majority view and highlight supporting passages. <cite id="c6a252b0-4">An extractive-Boolean QA approach for scientific fact checking combines automatic summarization with QA, highlighting texts from papers on a topic and achieving low error rates over millions of OA articles</cite>. This design emphasizes breadth and consensus-like coverage rather than selecting a single “greatest” item.

- Recency and impact signals: Several works and practice-oriented systems incorporate temporal and popularity heuristics—either explicitly weighting by publication date or by the recency/impact of citing literature. <cite id="ff036902-1">A review prioritizes recent and highly cited publications using a score that combines citation counts with exponential decay based on the year, emphasizing the significance of more recent citations</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">In biomedical search, classifiers can identify high-impact studies using time-agnostic features (e.g., journal impact factor, authorship, sample size) that perform similarly to time-sensitive approaches, and citation counts remain important when very recent citations are less critical</cite>. These design choices reflect real-world expectations that newer or more cited work may better reflect current consensus, but they also encode empirical regularities that can break down over time.

How systems prioritize in practice: signals, trade-offs, and abstention
- Signals and abstention: Empirical evaluations of scientific reasoning systems show that answering every question is risky; selective prediction and abstention reveal when evidence justifies an answer. <cite id="ff036902-2">SciFact and PubMedQA exhibit different operating regimes: risk rises sharply when models are forced to answer; risk-coverage analysis and abstention-aware evaluation better expose reliable decision-making and failure modes than accuracy alone</cite>. This underscores that systems often prioritize avoiding confident but unsupported claims over chasing any single signal (preponderance, recency, or strength).

- Coverage vs. strength: In domains like biomedical fact-checking over large OA corpora, breadth and multi-source aggregation dominate, with downstream QA models integrating many supporting snippets. <cite id="c6a252b0-4">Joint reasoning from facts and evidence across millions of OA articles highlights supporting passages and yields high accuracy, illustrating preponderance-style aggregation</cite>. By contrast, systems that explicitly select “strongest” supporting sentences for a given answer can be more efficient and robust when evidence conflicts. <cite id="c6a252b0-3">Agent-selected, convincing evidence improves plausibility across models/humans and supports correct answers with a tenth of the text</cite>.

- The role and pitfalls of recency: In clinical domains, “recent” is frequently used but inconsistently defined, which confounds recency-based prioritization. <cite id="ff036902-0">Across 1,000 biomedical articles, the median age of cited “recent” studies was only ~2–4 years, but lags ranged 0–37 years, with many references ≥10 years old; high-impact journals cited more up-to-date work</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">Moreover, time-agnostic features like journal impact and sample size can match time-based ranking of “high-impact” articles, suggesting that recency is not a stable proxy for quality or influence</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-4">At system scale, query-time recency can still be a measurable signal in citation surfaces, but its effect sizes vary with grouping definitions</cite>. Together, these findings imply that scientific QA systems that heavily weight recency risk either underrepresenting truly influential older work or overvaluing superficially “fresh” but low-quality items.

- Protocol vs. results and trustworthiness: When systems rely on raw protocol text or early-release summaries, answers can diverge from final trial results or pooled estimates. <cite id="e8fbb11c-1">Cochrane’s RoB 2 evaluates bias across domains including deviations from intended interventions and outcome selection (preregistered protocol vs reported outcomes), with all-low-risk domains indicating reliable results and any high-risk domain implying likely bias</cite>. <cite id="e8fbb11c-2">Systematic reviews may avoid GRADE certainty ratings and instead emphasize methodological quality and synthesis across designs, with explicit bias assessment procedures</cite>. These workflows show that QA systems which aggregate at protocol stage or rely on incomplete texts can misrepresent conclusions compared to meta-analyses based on completed outcomes.

Why measurement approaches conflict: effect estimation, bias, and selection
- Effect-size vs. p-value and sample size: Evidence aggregation can optimize different statistical targets, producing divergent answers. <cite id="e8fbb11c-3">Risk-of-bias tools differ in domains and thresholds (e.g., JBI for RCTs and quasi-experiments), and publication bias is assessed with funnel plots and Egger tests when sufficient studies are available</cite>. When systems prioritize effect-size pooling (meta-analysis) versus hypothesis tests (single-study confirmations), or overweight large samples and statistically significant p-values, they may endorse different claims than approaches that normalize for heterogeneity or emphasize robustness to bias.

- Subgroup vs. overall effects and missing outcomes: Real-world evidence surfaces selectively; QA systems trained on published summaries miss missing outcomes, selective reporting, and attrition. <cite id="e8fbb11c-2">Risk-of-bias assessments often reveal high risks in selection, performance, attrition, and other domains, undermining reliability of individual studies</cite>. <cite id="e8fbb11c-4">Meta-analytic examples show high risks of selection/performance/attrition bias in included RCTs</cite>. If QA pipelines aggregate based only on available text (e.g., published abstracts), they can favor studies with reported positive results and adequate sample sizes, conflicting with evidence that down-weights biased or incomplete reports.

- Citation-weighted vs. uniform-weight aggregation: Ranking by recent citations or impact can tilt conclusions toward popular or timely but potentially lower-quality literature. <cite id="ff036902-1">Weighting by recent citation counts and article-year yields different top-k sets than purely chronological ranking</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-0">Because “recent” in text can span decades, citation-based recency heuristics risk privileging items that read as “fresh” but are actually old</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">Conversely, time-agnostic features can recover high-impactness similarly well, suggesting that impact-based prioritization should be validated per domain rather than assumed to equal recency</cite>.

How evaluation choices yield conflicting conclusions
- Risk-coverage vs. accuracy: Metrics that encourage answering every query can inflate confident errors; abstention-aware evaluation reveals justified answers versus overconfident speculation. <cite id="ff036902-2">Forcing models to answer all questions in SciFact/PubMedQA causes rapid error increases; risk-coverage analysis better aligns with scientific reliability</cite>. Thus, systems evaluated for “maximum recall” may report different answers than those under abstention-aware or cost-sensitive regimes.

- Temporal slicing and concept drift: Benchmarks or retrieval strategies that freeze time vs. those that update to current citations produce different top-cited items and conclusions. <cite id="ff036902-0">Authors often label studies as “recent” yet cite items averaging 5.5 years old, with lags differing by specialty and journal impact</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">Time-agnostic classifiers match time-based approaches in predicting “high-impact” articles, indicating that recency alone may not drive long-term identification of influential work</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-1">Weighting schemes that decay by year emphasize recent citations, but their outputs depend on the chosen decay and time window</cite>.

- Corpus coverage and extraction method: Extractive-Boolean pipelines over OA corpora capture what is published and summarizable, whereas protocol-only or claim-matching pipelines miss later updates. <cite id="c6a252b0-4">A joint fact-and-evidence approach over 3M OA articles highlights supporting passages and achieves high F1, showing that breadth and extraction quality shape conclusions</cite>. <cite id="ff036902-3">Time-agnostic features can complement retrieval when very recent items are less important, but low recall limits surveillance use</cite>. These design choices can make a system appear “more up to date” or “more consensus-aligned” simply because it harvests a different slice of the literature.

Practical implications and design guidance
- Treat “recency” as a heuristic, not a rule: Systems should define “recent” concretely and, when possible, cross-check against completed reports and pooled estimates. <cite id="ff036902-0">Because “recent” spans 0–37-year gaps and is often used loosely, models that over-weight nominal recency risk misprioritizing evidence</cite>. <cite id="e8fbb11c-1">Bias assessments that distinguish protocol versus reported outcomes help detect when early-stage evidence conflicts with final results</cite>.

- Prefer strength + breadth with abstention: Combine multi-hop/convincingness selection with coverage-based fusion, and explicitly abstain when risk exceeds tolerance. <cite id="c6a252b0-3">Selecting the most convincing subset of sentences improves plausibility across models/humans</cite>; <cite id="c6a252b0-4">broad extractive-Boolean fusion over large OA corpora highlights supporting texts and achieves strong accuracy</cite>; <cite id="ff036902-2">abstention-aware evaluation reveals justified answers and reduces error under mis-specification</cite>.

- Align aggregation with measurement goals: If the question demands up-to-date guidance, prioritize protocols plus live updates and RoB checks; if it asks for consensus, weight by methodological quality and citation impact rather than raw recency. <cite id="e8fbb11c-2">Systematic reviews may avoid GRADE certainty ratings when the goal is synthesis across designs, focusing on explicit bias evaluation</cite>; <cite id="ff036902-1">citation-recency hybrids can surface current high-impact items, but their outputs vary with weighting choices</cite>.

- Make evaluation time-aware and sensitivity-aware: Compare results across frozen vs. rolling time windows, and report risk-coverage trade-offs, not just accuracy. <cite id="ff036902-2">Risk-coverage analysis exposes conditions under which models are justified to answer</cite>; <cite id="ff036902-0">recency definitions should consider observed citation lags by specialty and impact</cite>.

Open questions
- How to harmonize “strongest” and “preponderance” signals under uncertainty? Hybrid scorers that combine effect-size robustness, bias-adjusted weights, and abstention policies remain under-explored at system scale. <cite id="c6a252b0-3">Evidence selection based on convincingness generalizes across models/humans</cite>, yet its alignment with meta-analytic effect robustness needs principled integration. <cite id="ff036902-2">Abstention-aware evaluation is compelling</cite>, but policy tuning depends on application risk.

- How to operationalize “consensus” without overfitting to citation popularity? <cite id="ff036902-1">Recency-weighted citation counts bias toward high-cited, newer items</cite>, while <cite id="ff036902-3">time-agnostic impact features can be competitive</cite>, suggesting domain-specific calibrations and dynamic normalization of citation surfaces.

Conclusion
In practice, scientific QA systems do not purely follow preponderance, recency, or strongest-finding heuristics; rather, they blend coverage-based aggregation, selective “strongest” evidence extraction, and recency/impact signals, with explicit or implicit abstention policies that reveal when evidence is insufficient. <cite id="c6a252b0-4">Broad extractive-Boolean pipelines aggregate many sources</cite>, <cite id="c6a252b0-3">evidence-agent methods preferentially select convincing arguments</cite>, and <cite id="ff036902-2">abstention-aware evaluation clarifies justified answers</cite>. Divergent conclusions arise because measurement choices—effect pooling versus single-study tests, protocol-stage versus results-stage aggregation, RoB-graded versus popularity-weighted ranking, and frozen versus rolling time windows—encode different assumptions and expose different biases in the literature. <cite id="ff036902-0">Loose use of “recent”</cite>, <cite id="ff036902-3">concept drift in recency-impact mappings</cite>, and <cite id="e8fbb11c-1">protocol-to-results discrepancies</cite> all create conflict, underscoring the need for transparent, risk-aware, and time-aware evaluation to separate genuine consensus from artifact-driven aggregation. <cite id="ff036902-2">Abstention-aware and risk-coverage analyses are therefore central to reducing conflicting answers and improving trust</cite>. </answer>
